# Flex-Algo with SRv6: IGP Flexible Algorithm Guide

URL: https://srv6.md/topics/flex-algorithm/
Path: topics/flex-algorithm.md
Summary: IGP Flexible Algorithm (Flex-Algo, RFC 9350) with SRv6: per-algorithm locators, latency and TE metrics, network slicing, configuration and verification.

# Flex-Algorithm

**IGP Flexible Algorithm (Flex-Algo)** allows operators to define custom path computation algorithms within the IGP (IS-IS or OSPFv3). Combined with SRv6, it enables **network slicing** — multiple logical topologies over a single physical infrastructure.

## The Problem

Traditional IGP computes a single shortest path based on link metric. But modern networks need different paths for different services:

- **Voice/Video:** Lowest latency path
- **Bulk data:** Highest bandwidth path
- **Critical services:** Path avoiding certain nodes/links
- **Redundancy:** Disjoint paths for protection

## The Solution

Flex-Algo lets you define **multiple algorithms** (algo 128-255), each with its own:

- **Metric type** (IGP metric, latency, TE metric)
- **Constraints** (include/exclude affinities, SRLGs)
- **Calculation type** (SPF, strict SPF)

Each algorithm produces its own set of SRv6 SIDs, creating independent forwarding planes.

## How It Works

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[PE1] -->|10ms, BW:100G| B[P1]
    A -->|2ms, BW:10G| C[P2]
    B -->|5ms, BW:100G| D[PE2]
    C -->|3ms, BW:10G| D
```

| Algorithm | Metric | Best Path PE1→PE2 | Use Case |
|:---------:|--------|:------------------:|----------|
| **Algo 0** | IGP metric (default) | PE1→P2→PE2 | Default routing |
| **Algo 128** | Latency | PE1→P2→PE2 (5ms) | Low-latency services |
| **Algo 129** | TE metric (bandwidth) | PE1→P1→PE2 (100G) | High-bandwidth services |

### Per-Algorithm SRv6 Locators

Each Flex-Algo gets its own SRv6 locator, which means its own set of SIDs:

```
Node PE2 advertises:
  Algo 0:   fcbb:bb01:0002::/48  → Default IGP path
  Algo 128: fcbb:bb02:0002::/48  → Latency-optimized path
  Algo 129: fcbb:bb03:0002::/48  → Bandwidth-optimized path
```

To steer traffic on the low-latency path, simply use the Algo 128 SID as the destination. The IGP handles path computation automatically.

## Network Slicing with Flex-Algo

Flex-Algo is the foundation of **SRv6 network slicing** for 5G and enterprise services:

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph Physical Network
        direction LR
        R1[Router 1] --- R2[Router 2] --- R3[Router 3]
    end

    subgraph Slice 1 - Low Latency - Algo 128
        direction LR
        S1R1[R1] -.-> S1R2[R2] -.-> S1R3[R3]
    end

    subgraph Slice 2 - High BW - Algo 129
        direction LR
        S2R1[R1] -.-> S2R2[R2] -.-> S2R3[R3]
    end

    style S1R1 fill:#1565c026,stroke:#1565c0
    style S1R2 fill:#1565c026,stroke:#1565c0
    style S1R3 fill:#1565c026,stroke:#1565c0
    style S2R1 fill:#2e7d3226,stroke:#2e7d32
    style S2R2 fill:#2e7d3226,stroke:#2e7d32
    style S2R3 fill:#2e7d3226,stroke:#2e7d32
```

## Configuration

=== "Cisco IOS-XR"

    ```cisco
    !! Define Flex-Algo 128 (low latency)
    router isis CORE
     flex-algo 128
      metric-type delay
      advertise-definition
     !
     address-family ipv6 unicast
      segment-routing srv6
       locator LATENCY algo 128
      !
     !
    !

    !! Define SRv6 locator for Algo 128
    segment-routing
     srv6
      locators
       locator LATENCY
        micro-segment behavior unode psp-usd
        prefix fcbb:bb02::/48
        algorithm 128
       !
      !
     !
    !
    ```

=== "Juniper"

    ```junos
    set protocols isis source-packet-routing flex-algorithm 128
    set protocols isis source-packet-routing flex-algorithm 128 metric-type delay
    set routing-options source-packet-routing srv6 locator latency fcbb:bb02::/48 algorithm 128
    ```

## Flex-Algo Properties

| Property | Options | Description |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| **Algorithm ID** | 128-255 | User-defined algorithm number |
| **Metric Type** | IGP, delay, TE | Which metric to optimize |
| **Calculation Type** | SPF, Strict SPF | How to compute the path |
| **Include-any** | Admin groups | Links MUST have at least one of these affinities |
| **Include-all** | Admin groups | Links MUST have ALL of these affinities |
| **Exclude-any** | Admin groups | Links MUST NOT have any of these affinities |
| **Exclude SRLG** | SRLG values | Avoid links sharing a risk group |

## Verification

=== "Cisco IOS-XR"

    ```cisco
    show isis flex-algo 128
    show segment-routing srv6 locator LATENCY
    show isis route ipv6 fcbb:bb02:0002::/48 detail
    ```

=== "Juniper"

    ```junos
    show isis flex-algorithm 128
    show spring-traffic-engineering srv6-sid
    ```

!!! tip "Production validated"
    According to a [joint announcement by Cisco and SoftBank](https://news-blogs.cisco.com/apjc/2022/04/27/cisco-marks-worlds-first1-with-the-deployment-of-srv6-flex-algo-on-softbanks-5g-commercial-network/), SRv6 Flex-Algo was deployed on a commercial 5G network in April 2022.

# SRv6 L3VPN and EVPN: BGP Overlay Services (RFC 9252)

URL: https://srv6.md/topics/bgp-overlay-services/
Path: topics/bgp-overlay-services.md
Summary: How BGP delivers L3VPN and EVPN services over SRv6: overlay architecture, service SIDs, the BGP SRv6 Service TLV from RFC 9252, and verification commands.

# BGP Overlay Services over SRv6

SRv6 provides a clean, unified underlay for delivering **L3VPN** and **L2VPN (EVPN)** services using BGP — without MPLS, without LDP, without RSVP-TE. Just IPv6 + BGP.

## Architecture Overview

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph Overlay - BGP Control Plane
        BGP1[PE1 BGP] <-->|MP-BGP with SRv6 SIDs| BGP2[PE2 BGP]
    end

    subgraph Underlay - SRv6 Data Plane
        PE1[PE1] -->|SRv6 Transport| P1[P Node]
        P1 -->|SRv6 Transport| PE2[PE2]
    end

    CE1[CE1 - Customer] --- PE1
    CE2[CE2 - Customer] --- PE2
```

**Key principle:** BGP carries service information (VPN prefixes, EVPN routes) with SRv6 SIDs instead of MPLS labels. The SRv6 SID tells the remote PE exactly what to do with the packet (decap to which VRF, cross-connect to which interface, etc.).

## L3VPN over SRv6

### How It Works

1. **PE1** learns customer prefix `10.1.0.0/24` from CE1 in VRF `CUSTOMER-A`
2. **PE1** advertises via MP-BGP VPNv4/VPNv6 with an **SRv6 SID** instead of a VPN label:
    - Prefix: `10.1.0.0/24`
    - Next-Hop: `PE1 IPv6 address`
    - SRv6 Service SID: `fcbb:bb01:0001::DT4` (End.DT4 behavior)
3. **PE2** receives the BGP update, installs the route
4. When PE2 receives traffic for `10.1.0.0/24`, it encapsulates with:
    - IPv6 DA = `fcbb:bb01:0001::DT4`
    - Inner packet = original IPv4
5. **PE1** receives, matches End.DT4 SID, decapsulates, looks up in VRF `CUSTOMER-A`

### SRv6 SID Allocation Modes

| Mode | Description | SID per... |
|------|-------------|------------|
| **Per-VRF** | One SID shared by all prefixes in a VRF | VRF |
| **Per-CE** | One SID per CE neighbor | CE |
| **Per-Prefix** | Unique SID for each prefix | Prefix |

!!! tip "Per-VRF is most common"
    Per-VRF allocation (`End.DT4` / `End.DT6`) is the default and most scalable option. The SID says "decap and lookup in this VRF table."

### Configuration

=== "Cisco IOS-XR"

    ```cisco
    !! VRF definition
    vrf CUSTOMER-A
     address-family ipv4 unicast
      import route-target 100:1
      export route-target 100:1
     !
    !

    !! BGP with SRv6
    router bgp 65000
     address-family vpnv4 unicast
      segment-routing srv6
       locator MAIN
      !
     !
     vrf CUSTOMER-A
      rd 100:1
      address-family ipv4 unicast
       segment-routing srv6
        locator MAIN
        alloc mode per-vrf
       !
      !
     !
    !
    ```

=== "Juniper"

    ```junos
    set routing-instances CUSTOMER-A instance-type vrf
    set routing-instances CUSTOMER-A route-distinguisher 100:1
    set routing-instances CUSTOMER-A vrf-target target:100:1
    set routing-instances CUSTOMER-A protocols bgp source-packet-routing srv6 locator myloc
    ```

## EVPN over SRv6

EVPN (Ethernet VPN) provides L2 services (E-Line, E-LAN, E-Tree) and integrated L2/L3 services over SRv6 transport.

### EVPN Route Types with SRv6

| Route Type | Name | SRv6 Behavior |
|:----------:|------|---------------|
| **Type 2** | MAC/IP Advertisement | `End.DX2` or `End.DT2` |
| **Type 3** | Inclusive Multicast | BUM traffic handling |
| **Type 5** | IP Prefix Route | `End.DT4` / `End.DT6` (IP-VRF) |

### EVPN-VPWS (E-Line) with SRv6

Point-to-point L2 service using `End.DX2` behavior:

```
CE1 ──[L2 Frame]──► PE1 ──[IPv6(DA=PE2::DX2)][SRH][L2 Frame]──► PE2 ──[L2 Frame]──► CE2
```

The `End.DX2` SID tells PE2: "decapsulate and cross-connect this L2 frame to the specified attachment circuit."

### EVPN-VXLAN vs EVPN-SRv6

| Aspect | EVPN-VXLAN | EVPN-SRv6 |
|--------|:----------:|:---------:|
| Encapsulation | VXLAN (UDP) | SRv6 (IPv6 + SRH) |
| Underlay | IPv4 or IPv6 | IPv6 native |
| TE capability | Limited | Full SR Policy support |
| Network programming | None | Rich (service chaining, slicing) |
| MTU overhead | 50 bytes | 40 bytes (no SRH) to 56+ bytes (with SRH) |

## BGP SRv6 Service TLV (RFC 9252)

RFC 9252 defines how SRv6 SID information is carried in BGP updates using the **SRv6 Services TLVs** within the BGP Prefix-SID attribute:

```
BGP Update Message:
  ├── NLRI: 10.1.0.0/24 (VPNv4)
  ├── Next-Hop: 2001:db8::1
  ├── Extended Community: RT 100:1
  └── BGP Prefix-SID Attribute:
      └── SRv6 L3 Service TLV:
          ├── SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb01:0001::DT4
          ├── SRv6 SID Behavior: End.DT4 (19)
          └── SRv6 SID Structure:
              ├── Locator Block Length: 32
              ├── Locator Node Length: 16
              ├── Function Length: 16
              └── Argument Length: 0
```

### SID Transposition

To save space in BGP updates, the **function** part of the SID can be transposed into (encoded within) the VPN prefix itself, rather than carrying the full 128-bit SID. This is an optimization defined in RFC 9252.

## Verification

=== "Cisco IOS-XR"

    ```cisco
    !! Show VPNv4 routes with SRv6 SIDs
    show bgp vpnv4 unicast vrf CUSTOMER-A

    !! Show SRv6 SID details
    show segment-routing srv6 sid

    !! Show EVPN routes
    show bgp l2vpn evpn
    ```

=== "Linux (FRR)"

    ```bash
    vtysh -c "show bgp ipv4 vpn"
    vtysh -c "show bgp l2vpn evpn"
    vtysh -c "show segment-routing srv6 locator"
    ```

## References

1. [RFC 9252 - BGP Overlay Services Based on SRv6](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9252/) - Defines SRv6 Service TLVs in BGP for L3VPN, EVPN, and Internet services over SRv6

5. [Cisco XRdocs: SRv6 Transport on NCS5500 - Part 1](https://xrdocs.io/ncs5500/tutorials/srv6-transport-on-ncs-part-1) - Tutorial covering SRv6 transport fundamentals and L3VPN configuration on NCS 5500

# TI-LFA (RFC 9855): Segment Routing Fast Reroute Explained

URL: https://srv6.md/topics/ti-lfa/
Path: topics/ti-lfa.md
Summary: TI-LFA explained: P-space, Q-space and PQ nodes with a worked example, link vs node vs SRLG protection, RFC 9855, SRv6 repair, and Cisco IOS-XR, IOS-XE and Junos configs.

# TI-LFA (Topology Independent Loop-Free Alternate)

**Topology Independent Loop-Free Alternate — TI-LFA, sometimes written TILFA or "TI LFA" — is the fast-reroute (FRR) mechanism of Segment Routing.** Every router pre-computes, for each destination, a backup path that follows the route the network *will* use after the failure, and encodes it as a short segment list. When a link or neighbor fails, the router switches traffic onto that list in the data plane, without waiting for the IGP. It is standardized in [RFC 9855](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9855/) (October 2025, Proposed Standard) and works identically for SR-MPLS and SRv6.

TI-LFA builds on the older IP FRR ideas — LFA, Remote LFA and Directed LFA — and, in the RFC's words, extends them to "guaranteed coverage in any two-connected network". Segment Routing is what makes that possible: the repair router can steer a packet along *any* path with a couple of SIDs, so it never depends on a lucky neighbor.

## The Problem: The Convergence Window

When a link fails, the IGP must detect the failure, flood the change, run SPF and update the FIB on every affected router. Until that finishes — hundreds of milliseconds to seconds in a large network — packets toward the failed link are dropped or loop.

IP FRR closes that gap locally: the router next to the failure, the **Point of Local Repair (PLR)**, has a backup next hop pre-installed in its FIB and switches to it as soon as it detects the failure (loss of light, BFD). The question is where that backup path comes from.

| Mechanism | How the backup is found | Limitation |
|-----------|-------------------------|------------|
| **LFA** ([RFC 5286](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5286)) | A neighbor whose own shortest path to the destination does not come back through the PLR | Exists only if the topology happens to provide one. RFC 6571 measured per-prefix LFA coverage of **67–99%** (median 94%) across 11 service-provider cores |
| **Remote LFA** ([RFC 7490](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7490)) | Tunnel (LDP) to a remote "PQ node" from which traffic flows to the destination unaided | Still topology-dependent: RFC 7490 reports **97.5–100%** link coverage on 14 topologies and much lower guaranteed node protection |
| **TI-LFA** (RFC 9855) | Segment list that reproduces the post-convergence path | Needs Segment Routing and enough SID depth on the PLR; covers any two-connected topology |

## Key Terms

| Term | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| **PLR** | Point of Local Repair — the router adjacent to the failure that switches traffic to the backup |
| **Protected resource (X)** | The link, node or SRLG the backup must avoid |
| **Post-convergence path** | The shortest path from the PLR to the destination once X is removed from the topology. TI-LFA repairs onto this path, so traffic does not move again when the IGP converges |
| **P-space P(R,X)** | Routers the PLR R can reach on its normal (pre-failure) shortest paths without any of those paths — including ECMP splits — crossing X |
| **Extended P-space** | The union of the P-spaces of the PLR's neighbors (except those reached via X). A router in the extended P-space can be reached by sending the packet out a specific neighbor first |
| **Q-space Q(D,X)** | Routers whose normal shortest path to the destination D does not cross X. A packet dropped off at a Q node gets to D on its own |
| **PQ node** | A node in both the (extended) P-space and the Q-space ([RFC 7490](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7490) §1.1). A single segment to a PQ node is a complete repair |
| **Repair list (RL)** | The segments the PLR adds to the packet — generically `` |

## Worked Example: Finding P, Q and the Repair List

Six routers, IS-IS metrics on the links. S is the PLR, protecting its link to N, for traffic to D.

```mermaid
graph LR
    S((S)) ---|10 · protected| N((N))
    N ---|10| D((D))
    S ---|10| A((A))
    A ---|10| B((B))
    B ---|40| C((C))
    C ---|10| D
```

**Before the failure**, S reaches D via N (cost 20). A also reaches D via S and N (cost 30), so A is **not** an LFA: by the RFC 5286 inequality, A is loop-free only if dist(A,D) < dist(A,S) + dist(S,D), i.e. 30 < 10 + 20, which is false. Classic LFA has nothing to offer here.

**Step 1 — post-convergence path.** Remove S–N and recompute: S → A → B → C → D, cost 70.

**Step 2 — P-space of S (avoiding S–N).**

| Node | Shortest path from S today | Crosses S–N? | In P-space? |
|------|---------------------------|:------------:|:-----------:|
| A | S→A (10) | No | |
| B | S→A→B (20) | No | |
| C | S→N→D→C (30) | Yes | — |
| D | S→N→D (20) | Yes | — |

Extended P-space adds what A can reach without S–N: B, but not C (A's shortest path to C, cost 40, goes back through S–N). Extended P-space = {A, B}.

**Step 3 — Q-space of D (avoiding S–N).**

| Node | Shortest path to D today | Crosses S–N? | In Q-space? |
|------|--------------------------|:------------:|:-----------:|
| C | C→D (10) | No | |
| B | B→A→S→N→D (40), cheaper than B→C→D (50) | Yes | — |
| A | A→S→N→D (30) | Yes | — |

**Step 4 — intersect along the post-convergence path.** P nodes on the path: A, B. Q nodes on the path: C. There is no PQ node, but the last P node (B) and the first Q node (C) are **adjacent**. RFC 9855 §5.3 gives the repair list:

```text
RL = < Node-SID(B), Adj-SID(B→C) >
```

The adjacency SID is essential: if S only sent the packet to B, B would forward it on its own shortest path to D — back through A and S — and the packet would loop. The Adj-SID forces B to use the expensive B–C link, after which C's normal routing delivers it.

!!! example "Variation: a PQ node exists"
    Lower the B–C metric to 10. Now B's own shortest path to D is B→C→D (20), so B is in the Q-space as well as the P-space. B is a **PQ node** and the repair list shrinks to a single segment: `RL = ` — exactly what Remote LFA would have found, but without an LDP tunnel.

In SRv6 the same list becomes SRv6 SIDs: B's End (uN) SID followed by B's End.X (uA) SID toward C. With [uSID](https://srv6.md/topics/usid-compression/) both fit in one 128-bit container, so the PLR adds a single outer IPv6 header and no SRH:

```text
Original packet at S:   IPv6(DA = D's service SID) | payload
Repaired at S:          IPv6(DA = fcbb:bb00:B:BC::) | IPv6(DA = D's service SID) | payload
                                    └uN(B) └uA(B→C)
At B:  uN shifts, uA forwards over B–C and, with PSP/USD, removes the outer header
At C:  plain IPv6 forwarding of the original packet to D
```

### Repair-list shapes (RFC 9855 Section 5)

| Case | RFC 9855 | Repair list | Comparable to |
|------|----------|-------------|---------------|
| A direct neighbor is on the post-convergence path and in P and Q | §5.1 | Empty — just a different outgoing interface | Post-convergence LFA |
| A PQ node exists | §5.2 | `` | Remote LFA |
| P and Q are adjacent | §5.3 | `` | Directed LFA |
| P and Q are distant | §5.4 | `` (implementation-specific optimization) | — |

How often each case occurs is measured in RFC 9855 Appendix B on nine real networks: for link and local-SRLG protection, **one SID or fewer covers more than 99%** of destinations; for node protection, two SIDs or fewer cover 99%. On SRv6, adjacency SIDs are globally routable, so the list is often even shorter than on SR-MPLS (§7.2).

## Link vs Node vs SRLG Protection

The algorithm is the same; what changes is the resource X removed from the topology before computing the post-convergence path, P-space and Q-space.

| Protection | Removes from the topology | Repair-list effect | Use when |
|------------|---------------------------|--------------------|----------|
| **Link** (default) | The primary link S–N | Shortest lists; the backup may still pass **through N** via another link | Fiber cuts, optics failures |
| **Node** | N and all its links | Can need one more SID than link protection; never uses N | Router crashes, linecard resets, maintenance |
| **SRLG** | Every local link sharing an SRLG with S–N | Avoids links in the same conduit, DWDM system or linecard | Shared infrastructure failures |

Two things are easy to miss:

- **A link-protecting backup can be useless for a node failure.** If S has two parallel links to N, the link-protecting backup for one of them is simply the other — which dies too if N reboots. Node protection forces the list around N. If no node-protecting path exists, implementations fall back to link protection.
- **Node protection only protects transit through N.** Traffic whose destination *is* N (or a service SID owned by N) cannot be rerouted around N; RFC 9855 §6.1 keeps an active node segment on the packet and adds the repair list in front of it. Protecting traffic to a failed egress PE is a separate problem (see [draft-ietf-rtgwg-srv6-egress-protection](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-rtgwg-srv6-egress-protection/) and BGP PIC).

Vendors pick between the modes with **tiebreakers**. A node-protecting path is preferred only when you configure it. Check SRLG support per data plane: Junos ignores SRLG in SRv6 TI-LFA and does not support SRLG protection in IPv6 networks.

## How TI-LFA Works with SRv6

RFC 9855 §7.2 states that the computation is identical for SRv6; only the encoding differs:

- At a **transit** PLR, the repair list is added with a headend behavior from RFC 8986 §5 — typically **H.Encaps.Red**, an outer IPv6 header whose DA is the first repair SID.
- At a PLR that is itself a **segment endpoint** for the packet, it first executes its endpoint behavior and then protects the packet like a transit packet.
- Repair SIDs advertised with the **USD** (and PSP) flavor let the last repair node remove the outer header and forward the original packet. That is why Cisco shows the P node's SID as `uN (PSP/USD)`.

Implementations differ in how the repair is applied, so don't assume one behavior:

| Platform | Repair encoding shown in the FIB |
|----------|----------------------------------|
| Cisco 8000 (IOS-XR) | `SRv6 H.Encaps.Red SID-list {…}`; with full-length SIDs, a backup is installed only if it needs two SIDs or fewer |
| Cisco NCS 5500/540 (IOS-XR) | `SRv6 H.Insert.Red SID-list {…}` (SRH insertion) |
| Cisco IOS-XE | `Segment List … mode:insert` |
| Junos | Encapsulation (reduced SRH) at the ingress PE; SRH insertion at transit nodes with `transit-srh-insert` |

## Configuration

=== "Cisco IOS-XR (SRv6)"

    ```cisco
    segment-routing
     srv6
      locators
       locator MAIN
        micro-segment behavior unode psp-usd
        prefix fcbb:bb00:1::/48
    !
    router isis CORE
     address-family ipv6 unicast
      metric-style wide
      microloop avoidance segment-routing
      segment-routing srv6
       locator MAIN
     !
     interface HundredGigE0/0/0/1
      point-to-point
      address-family ipv6 unicast
       fast-reroute per-prefix
       fast-reroute per-prefix ti-lfa
       !! optional: prefer node-protecting, then SRLG-disjoint backups
       fast-reroute per-prefix tiebreaker node-protecting index 100
       fast-reroute per-prefix tiebreaker srlg-disjoint index 200
    ```

    Link protection is the default. On current releases a **lower index means a higher priority** (range 1–255), and link protection always ranks below node or SRLG protection. Some older material, such as the 2016 SR TI-LFA TOI, describes the opposite ordering, so check the guide for your release. For SR-MPLS, configure the same `fast-reroute` commands under `address-family ipv4 unicast` with `segment-routing mpls`. To exclude a Flex-Algo from protection, use `flex-algo 128` → `fast-reroute disable`.

=== "Cisco IOS-XE"

    ```cisco
    !! SR-MPLS TI-LFA
    router isis
     fast-reroute per-prefix level-2 all
     fast-reroute ti-lfa level-2
     fast-reroute tie-break level-2 node-protecting 100
    !
    interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1
     isis network point-to-point
    !
    !! SRv6 TI-LFA (IOS XE 17.15.1a and later)
    segment-routing srv6
     locators
      locator A
       prefix CAFE:0:601::/48
       format usid-f3216
    !
    router isis 1
     address-family ipv6
      multi-topology
      segment-routing srv6
       locator A
      fast-reroute per-prefix level-2 all
      fast-reroute ti-lfa level-2
     exit-address-family
    ```

    Interface-level `isis fast-reroute ti-lfa protection level-2` overrides the protocol default and `... disable` excludes an interface. Default tiebreakers are linecard-disjoint, lowest-backup-metric and srlg-disjoint; node-protecting must be enabled explicitly. Cisco notes that IGP TI-LFA on IOS-XE "cannot guarantee 50 ms". See also [Cisco IOS-XE](https://srv6.md/implementations/cisco-ios-xe/).

=== "Junos"

    ```junos
    # TI-LFA for SR-MPLS and SRv6 in IS-IS
    set protocols isis backup-spf-options use-post-convergence-lfa
    set protocols isis backup-spf-options use-post-convergence-lfa maximum-backup-paths 2
    set protocols isis backup-spf-options use-source-packet-routing
    set protocols isis interface et-0/0/1.0 level 2 post-convergence-lfa
    # optional, per interface
    set protocols isis interface et-0/0/1.0 level 2 post-convergence-lfa node-protection
    set protocols isis interface et-0/0/1.0 level 2 post-convergence-lfa srlg-protection   # SR-MPLS/IPv4 only

    # SRv6 microloop avoidance
    set protocols isis spf-options microloop-avoidance post-convergence-path delay 5000
    ```

    Link protection is the default once `post-convergence-lfa` is on an interface. `maximum-labels` (2–5, default 3) caps the MPLS repair stack and `maximum-backup-paths` (1–8, default 1) the number of backups. For SRv6, Junos encapsulates with a reduced SRH at the ingress PE and can insert an SRH at transit nodes with `transit-srh-insert`. Micro-SID support for SRv6 TI-LFA and microloop avoidance arrived in Junos 23.4R1 (MX). `srlg-protection` (MX/PTX, 20.2R1) does not apply to SRv6: SRv6 TI-LFA ignores SRLGs, and SRLG protection is not supported in IPv6 or multi-topology networks. See [Juniper](https://srv6.md/implementations/juniper/) for the full SRv6 setup.

## Verification

=== "Cisco IOS-XR"

    ```cisco
    show isis ipv6 fast-reroute fcbb:bb00:2::/48 detail
    !! Backup path: TI-LFA (link), via fe80::..., HundredGigE0/0/0/1 Node3, Metric: 40
    !!   P node: Node4.00 [...], SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb00:4:: uN (PSP/USD)

    show route ipv6 fcbb:bb00:2::/48 detail
    !!   ... Backup (TI-LFA)   Repair Node(s): ...
    !!   SRv6 Headend: H.Encaps.Red, SID-list {fcbb:bb00:4::}

    show cef ipv6 fcbb:bb00:2::/48 detail
    show cef ipv6 fast-reroute-db
    ```

    The protection type appears in parentheses: `TI-LFA (link)`, `(node)`, `(srlg)` or `(node+srlg)`. On SR-MPLS, `show isis fast-reroute  detail` lists the P and Q nodes with their labels, and `show cef` shows the imposed label stack.

=== "Cisco IOS-XE"

    ```cisco
    show isis fast-reroute ti-lfa tunnel          ! SR-MPLS repair tunnels
    show ip cef 10.0.0.2 internal
    show isis ipv6 fast-reroute summary            ! SRv6: protected prefixes and coverage
    show isis ipv6 rib fcbb:bb00:2::/48            ! "repair path: via ... (DS,NP)"
    show ipv6 cef fcbb:bb00:2::/48 internal        ! "Segment List ... mode:insert"
    show isis ipv6 fast-reroute ti-lfa fwd-ids
    ```

=== "Junos"

    ```junos
    show isis backup coverage            # % of nodes and prefixes protected per address family
    show isis backup spf results         # backup computation per destination
    show isis backup spf results no-coverage
    show route 2001:db8::2 extensive     # primary and backup next hops
    ```

## TI-LFA and Micro-Loops

TI-LFA protects the moment of failure at the PLR. It does nothing for the **micro-loops** that can form elsewhere while routers update their FIBs at different times, or when the link comes back. RFC 9855 §1 calls the two mechanisms complementary and warns of one interaction: if the PLR converges early and releases its TI-LFA path before its neighbors have converged, the packets that were safely on the repair path can start looping — especially for repairs built from §5.2–5.4 (PQ or P/Q nodes rather than a direct neighbor).

The usual fix is to keep the TI-LFA path in place for a while after local convergence ([RFC 8333](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8333)-style local delay) or to steer traffic over a loop-free SR path until the network settles:

```cisco
router isis CORE
 address-family ipv6 unicast
  microloop avoidance segment-routing
  microloop avoidance rib-update-delay 5000
```

On IOS-XR the delay range is documented as 1–60000 ms with a default of 5000. See [Micro-Loop Avoidance](https://srv6.md/topics/micro-loop-avoidance/) for the full picture.

!!! note "TI-LFA for multicast: RFC 9860"
    TI-LFA repair paths can also protect **PIM** trees. [RFC 9860](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9860/) (October 2025, Informational) uses the repair segment list to build the MoFRR standby tree: the P-node's End SID is translated into a PIM RPF Vector and the P→Q End.X SID into an Explicit RPF Vector, so the secondary join follows the repair path hop by hop. This gives MoFRR the same topology-independent coverage that TI-LFA gives unicast. See [Multicast & Broadcast](https://srv6.md/topics/multicast/).

## TI-LFA vs Other FRR Mechanisms

| Mechanism | Coverage (published data) | Extra state | Repair follows post-convergence path | Topology dependent |
|-----------|---------------------------|-------------|:-----------------------------------:|:------------------:|
| **LFA** (RFC 5286) | 67–99% per prefix (RFC 6571, 11 SP cores) | None | Not necessarily | Yes |
| **Remote LFA** (RFC 7490) | 97.5–100% link protection (RFC 7490, 14 topologies) | Targeted LDP sessions | Not necessarily | Yes |
| **TI-LFA** (RFC 9855) | Any two-connected network; >99% with ≤ 1 SID for link protection (RFC 9855 App. B) | None beyond SR SIDs | Yes | No |
| **RSVP-TE FRR** | Full, per protected LSP | Bypass/detour LSPs and RSVP state | No | No |

!!! tip "No extra protocol state"
    TI-LFA needs no tunnels, no RSVP and no targeted LDP: the IGP computes the repair lists from the SIDs it already advertises. What it does need is enough **SID depth** on the PLR (some platforms install a backup only if it fits in two SIDs) and the protected SIDs advertised by every node on the repair path.

# SRv6 SR Policy: ODN, Color Steering and Binding SID

URL: https://srv6.md/topics/sr-policy/
Path: topics/sr-policy.md
Summary: SRv6 traffic engineering with SR Policies — ODN, PCE, Binding SID, color steering, and dynamic path computation

# SR Policy

**SR Policy** is the framework for expressing traffic engineering intent in Segment Routing networks (RFC 9256). Instead of hop-by-hop RSVP-TE signaling, an SR Policy encodes the entire path as a segment list at the headend — no per-flow state on transit nodes.

## The Problem

RSVP-TE provides path control but requires:

- **Per-tunnel state on every transit router** — signaling messages, path maintenance, bandwidth reservations
- **Multiple protocols** — RSVP for tunnels, IGP for routing, PCEP for computation
- **Scalability limits** — thousands of tunnels degrade control plane performance
- **Slow convergence** — path recomputation and re-signaling on failure

SR Policy eliminates distributed state by encoding the path in the packet header itself.

## SR Policy Architecture (RFC 9256)

An SR Policy is identified by a tuple of **(headend, color, endpoint)**:

| Component | Description | Example |
|-----------|-------------|---------|
| **Headend** | Router originating the policy | PE1 (`2001:db8::1`) |
| **Color** | Numeric intent identifier (community) | `100` (low-latency) |
| **Endpoint** | Destination of the policy | PE2 (`2001:db8::2`) |

### Candidate Paths

Each SR Policy contains one or more **candidate paths**, ordered by preference. Only the highest-preference valid path is active.

```
SR Policy (headend=PE1, color=100, endpoint=PE2)
  ├── Candidate Path (preference 200, PCE-computed)
  │     └── Segment List: [P1::1, P3::1, PE2::1]
  ├── Candidate Path (preference 150, BGP SR Policy)
  │     └── Segment List: [P2::1, PE2::1]
  └── Candidate Path (preference 100, local config)
        └── Segment List: [PE2::1]
```

Each candidate path can contain multiple **segment lists** with weights for weighted ECMP load balancing.

### SR Policy Lifecycle

```mermaid
graph TD
    H[Headend Router] -->|1. Policy created| CP1[Candidate Path 1 - Pref 200]
    H -->|1. Policy created| CP2[Candidate Path 2 - Pref 100]
    CP1 -->|2. Validated| SL1[Segment List A - Weight 50]
    CP1 -->|2. Validated| SL2[Segment List B - Weight 50]
    CP2 -->|Standby| SL3[Segment List C]
    SL1 -->|3. Active - ECMP| FWD[Forwarding]
    SL2 -->|3. Active - ECMP| FWD
```

## Policy Instantiation Methods

SR Policies can be created through three mechanisms, each with a default preference:

| Method | Default Preference | Source | Use Case |
|--------|:-----------------:|--------|----------|
| **Local configuration** | 100 | CLI / YANG | Static TE, fallback paths |
| **BGP SR Policy (SAFI 73)** | 100-200 | Controller / RR | Multi-domain, centralized TE |
| **PCEP** | 200 | SR-PCE | Dynamic computation, bandwidth-aware |

### Local Configuration

Explicit segment lists defined on the headend. Simple, static, and useful as a fallback.

=== "Cisco IOS-XR"

    ```cisco
    segment-routing
     traffic-eng
      policy LOW-LATENCY-TO-PE2
       color 100 end-point ipv6 2001:db8::2
       candidate-paths
        preference 100
         explicit segment-list VIA-P1-P3
        !
       !
      !
      segment-list VIA-P1-P3
       index 10 srv6 sid fc00:0:1::
       index 20 srv6 sid fc00:0:3::
       index 30 srv6 sid fc00:0:2::
      !
     !
    !
    ```

=== "Juniper"

    ```junos
    set protocols source-packet-routing segment-list VIA-P1-P3 srv6 hop1 sid fc00:0:1::
    set protocols source-packet-routing segment-list VIA-P1-P3 srv6 hop2 sid fc00:0:3::
    set protocols source-packet-routing segment-list VIA-P1-P3 srv6 hop3 sid fc00:0:2::
    set protocols source-packet-routing sr-policy LOW-LATENCY-TO-PE2 color 100
    set protocols source-packet-routing sr-policy LOW-LATENCY-TO-PE2 end-point 2001:db8::2
    set protocols source-packet-routing sr-policy LOW-LATENCY-TO-PE2 segment-list VIA-P1-P3
    ```

### BGP SR Policy (SAFI 73)

A controller or route reflector distributes SR Policies via BGP using the SR Policy SAFI. This enables centralized traffic engineering across multiple domains.

The BGP update carries:

- **Distinguisher + Policy Color + Endpoint** as NLRI
- **Tunnel Encapsulation attribute** with segment lists, preference, binding SID

### PCE-Initiated Policies

An SR-PCE (Path Computation Element) computes constrained paths using topology learned via BGP-LS (RFC 9514) and installs them on headends via PCEP.

```mermaid
graph LR
    BGP_LS[BGP-LS Topology] -->|RFC 9514| PCE[SR-PCE Controller]
    PCE -->|PCEP - Computed Path| PE1[Headend PE1]
    PE1 -->|SRv6 Segment List| P1[P1]
    P1 --> P3[P3]
    P3 --> PE2[Egress PE2]
```

=== "Cisco IOS-XR"

    ```cisco
    !! PCE configuration on headend
    segment-routing
     traffic-eng
      pcc
       source-address ipv6 2001:db8::1
       pce address ipv6 2001:db8:ffff::1
        precedence 10
       !
      !
     !
    !
    ```

## On-Demand Nexthop (ODN)

ODN dynamically creates SR Policies when a BGP prefix with a **color community** is received, without any pre-provisioned policy on the headend. This is the most operationally scalable approach.

### How ODN Works

1. Remote PE advertises a VPN prefix with a **color extended community** (e.g., color 100)
2. Local PE receives the prefix and matches it against an **ODN template** for that color
3. If no SR Policy exists for that (color, endpoint), the headend **automatically** creates one
4. The policy is computed locally or delegated to PCE based on template configuration

```mermaid
graph LR
    CE1[CE1] --> PE1[PE1 - Headend]
    PE1 -->|ODN creates SR Policy| CORE((SRv6 Core))
    CORE --> PE2[PE2 - Egress]
    PE2 --> CE2[CE2]
    PE2 -.->|BGP: prefix + color 100| PE1
```

### ODN Configuration

=== "Cisco IOS-XR"

    ```cisco
    !! ODN template for color 100 (low-latency)
    segment-routing
     traffic-eng
      on-demand color 100
       dynamic
        metric type latency
       !
       srv6
        locator MAIN
       !
      !
     !
    !

    !! ODN with PCE delegation
    segment-routing
     traffic-eng
      on-demand color 200
       dynamic
        pcep
        !
        metric type te
       !
      !
     !
    !
    ```

=== "Juniper"

    ```junos
    set protocols source-packet-routing sr-preference-override color 100 routing-policy LOW-LATENCY
    set policy-options policy-statement LOW-LATENCY term 1 then install-nexthop lsp-regex ".*"
    ```

## Binding SID (BSID)

A Binding SID is a **single SID that represents an entire SR Policy**. Any packet arriving with a BSID as the active segment is steered into the associated policy's segment list.

### Key Properties

| Property | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| **Abstraction** | Hides the internal path — remote domains only see one SID |
| **Scalability** | Reduces segment list depth for multi-domain paths |
| **Stitching** | Chains policies across domains: `[BSID-Domain1, BSID-Domain2]` |
| **Dynamic** | BSID can be allocated dynamically and signaled via BGP or PCEP |

### Multi-Domain BSID Chaining

```
Ingress segment list:  [BSID_AS1, BSID_AS2, PE-Remote::DT4]

At AS1 border:  BSID_AS1 expands to [P1::1, ASBR1::1]
At AS2 border:  BSID_AS2 expands to [P5::1, PE-Remote::1]
```

=== "Cisco IOS-XR"

    ```cisco
    segment-routing
     traffic-eng
      policy TO-AS2
       binding-sid srv6 dynamic behavior ub6-insert-reduced
       color 500 end-point ipv6 2001:db8:2::1
       candidate-paths
        preference 100
         explicit segment-list VIA-ASBR
        !
       !
      !
     !
    !
    ```

!!! tip "BSID and inter-domain TE"
    For a deep dive into Binding SID for multi-domain traffic engineering, see [Inter-Domain SRv6](https://srv6.md/topics/inter-domain/). For BSID in the context of SR-MPLS/SRv6 migration, see [Interworking & Migration](https://srv6.md/topics/interworking-migration/).

## Color Steering

BGP color extended communities map **service intent** to SR Policies. When a VPN prefix carries a color, the headend PE automatically steers traffic into the matching SR Policy.

| Color | Intent | Mechanism |
|:-----:|--------|-----------|
| 100 | Low latency | Flex-Algo 128 or SR Policy with latency metric |
| 200 | High bandwidth | Flex-Algo 129 or SR Policy with bandwidth constraint |
| 300 | Disjoint paths | Pair of SR Policies with disjointness constraint |
| 400 | Cost-optimized | Default IGP metric (best-cost path) |

### How Color Steering Works

1. Customer VRF route is received via BGP with `color:100` extended community
2. Headend PE looks up SR Policy with `(color=100, endpoint=BGP-next-hop)`
3. If found → traffic is steered into the policy
4. If not found + ODN enabled → policy is created on demand

!!! warning "Color values are locally significant"
    Color values have no global meaning — operators define their own mapping between color values and intent. Consistent color assignment across the network is an operational requirement.

## Dynamic Path Computation

SR Policies can be computed dynamically based on **optimization objectives** and **constraints**:

### Optimization Objectives

| Objective | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| **TE metric** | Minimize traffic engineering metric (admin-defined) |
| **Latency** | Minimize end-to-end delay |
| **Hop count** | Minimize number of nodes traversed |
| **IGP metric** | Minimize standard IGP cost |

### Constraints

| Constraint | Description |
|------------|-------------|
| **Affinity (include/exclude)** | Links must match color/admin-group requirements |
| **SRLG** | Path must avoid specific shared risk link groups |
| **Bandwidth** | Path must have minimum available bandwidth |
| **Disjointness** | Two policies must not share links/nodes/SRLGs |

### Reoptimization

Dynamic policies can be reoptimized when:

- Topology changes (link up/down, metric change)
- Periodic timer expires
- Bandwidth threshold crossed
- Manual trigger

## Verification

=== "Cisco IOS-XR"

    ```cisco
    !! Show all SR Policies
    show segment-routing traffic-eng policy summary

    !! Show specific policy details
    show segment-routing traffic-eng policy color 100 endpoint ipv6 2001:db8::2

    !! Show ODN policies
    show segment-routing traffic-eng policy on-demand

    !! Show BSID allocation
    show segment-routing traffic-eng binding-sid

    !! Show PCE-delegated policies
    show segment-routing traffic-eng pcc
    ```

=== "Juniper"

    ```junos
    show spring-traffic-engineering lsp
    show spring-traffic-engineering lsp detail
    show spring-traffic-engineering lsp color 100
    ```

## SR Policy vs RSVP-TE

| Aspect | RSVP-TE | SR Policy |
|--------|---------|-----------|
| **Transit state** | Per-tunnel on every hop | None — path in packet header |
| **Signaling** | RSVP PATH/RESV per tunnel | BGP / PCEP / local config |
| **Scalability** | 10K tunnels typical limit | 100K+ policies (headend only) |
| **FRR** | Facility backup (manual) | TI-LFA (automatic, 100% coverage) |
| **Bandwidth** | RSVP admission control | PCE-based or Flex-Algo |
| **Multi-domain** | Complex (inter-AS RSVP) | BSID stitching (simple) |
| **Automation** | Limited | ODN + color steering (intent-based) |

- [Flex-Algorithm](https://srv6.md/topics/flex-algorithm/) — Constraint-based topology slicing
- [TI-LFA](https://srv6.md/topics/ti-lfa/) — Fast reroute for SR Policies

- [RFC 9857](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9857/) — Reporting SR Policy state via BGP-LS

# SRv6 Micro-Loop Avoidance During IGP Convergence

URL: https://srv6.md/topics/micro-loop-avoidance/
Path: topics/micro-loop-avoidance.md
Summary: Preventing transient forwarding loops during IGP convergence using SRv6 local delay and explicit post-convergence paths

# Micro-Loop Avoidance

After a link or node failure, IGP routers recompute their forwarding tables at different times. During this convergence window (200ms-2s), routers may temporarily disagree on the best path — creating **transient forwarding loops** called micro-loops.

## What Are Micro-Loops?

### The Problem

When a topology change occurs, each router independently runs SPF and updates its FIB. Routers closer to the failure detect and converge faster than distant routers. This temporal mismatch creates loops:

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[R1 - Converged] -->|Sends to R2| B[R2 - Not yet converged]
    B -->|Sends back to R1| A
    C[R3] -->|X FAIL| D[R4]
```

**Timeline of a micro-loop:**

1. **T=0ms:** Link R3-R4 fails
2. **T=10ms:** R3 detects failure, reconverges, now forwards via R1
3. **T=10-500ms:** R1 has **not yet reconverged** — still points to R2 for the destination
4. **R1 → R2 → R1 → R2...** — packets loop until R1 and R2 both converge
5. **T=500ms-2s:** All routers converge, loop stops

### Impact

| Effect | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Packet loss** | TTL expiry after 64-255 hops in the loop |
| **Bandwidth waste** | Looping packets consume link capacity |
| **Jitter** | Surviving traffic experiences delay spikes |
| **CPU load** | High packet rate from loops stresses forwarding engines |

## TI-LFA vs Micro-Loop Avoidance

TI-LFA and micro-loop avoidance solve **different phases** of convergence:

```mermaid
graph LR
    FAIL[Failure] --> TILFA[TI-LFA Backup<br/>0 - 50ms]
    TILFA --> MLA[Micro-Loop Window<br/>50ms - 2s]
    MLA --> CONV[Fully Converged]
```

| Aspect | TI-LFA | Micro-Loop Avoidance |
|--------|--------|---------------------|
| **Purpose** | Instant backup path at failure-adjacent node | Prevent loops during network-wide convergence |
| **Coverage window** | 0-50ms (detection + switchover) | 50ms-2s (IGP convergence) |
| **Scope** | Local to the detecting router | Network-wide coordination |
| **Prerequisite** | SRv6 SIDs | TI-LFA (to carry traffic during delay) |

!!! warning "Without TI-LFA, micro-loop avoidance causes blackholes"
    Micro-loop avoidance works by **delaying FIB updates**. Without TI-LFA providing a backup path during that delay, traffic would be blackholed. Always enable TI-LFA first.

## Solution 1: Local Delay (Recommended)

The simplest and most widely deployed approach. Each router **delays its FIB update** by a configurable timer after receiving a topology change notification. TI-LFA carries traffic during the delay.

### How It Works

1. Router receives LSP/LSA indicating topology change
2. Router runs SPF and computes new paths, but **does not update FIB yet**
3. TI-LFA backup path carries traffic (installed at failure detection time)
4. After the delay timer expires (e.g., 5000ms), FIB is updated
5. By this time, all routers have converged — no loop

### Why SRv6 Makes This Work

In traditional IP/LDP networks, delaying the FIB update means traffic is **blackholed** because there's no backup path. With SRv6 + TI-LFA:

- TI-LFA pre-computes a loop-free backup path using SRv6 SIDs
- Traffic switches to the backup in <50ms
- The backup carries traffic for the entire delay window
- When FIB updates, traffic moves to the new primary path seamlessly

### Configuration

=== "Cisco IOS-XR"

    ```cisco
    !! Enable micro-loop avoidance with segment-routing
    router isis CORE
     address-family ipv6 unicast
      microloop avoidance segment-routing
      microloop avoidance rib-update-delay 5000
     !
    !
    ```

=== "Juniper"

    ```junos
    set protocols isis spf-options microloop-avoidance post-convergence-path delay 5000
    ```

## Solution 2: Explicit Post-Convergence Path

Instead of delaying the FIB update, the router **immediately installs the new path** but encodes it as an **explicit SRv6 segment list** that is loop-free by construction (source-routed paths cannot loop).

### How It Works

1. Router computes the post-convergence shortest path
2. Encodes the path as an SRv6 segment list (node SIDs of intermediate hops)
3. Installs this explicit path immediately — no delay needed
4. After all routers converge, switches to the native shortest path (removes explicit segments)

### Advantage

No delay timer needed — convergence is immediate and loop-free. The trade-off is slightly more SRH overhead during the convergence window.

=== "Cisco IOS-XR"

    ```cisco
    router isis CORE
     address-family ipv6 unicast
      microloop avoidance segment-routing
     !
    !
    ```

## Solution 3: Ordered FIB (oFIB)

Routers update their FIBs in a **coordinated order** based on their distance from the failure. Routers farther from the failure update first, then progressively closer routers update.

| Pros | Cons |
|------|------|
| No SRv6 dependency | Slower convergence (ordered updates) |
| Works with any forwarding plane | Complex to implement correctly |
| No additional header overhead | Not widely deployed |

!!! info "oFIB is rarely used in practice"
    Most SRv6 deployments use **local delay** (Solution 1) because it is simpler and TI-LFA is already required for fast reroute.

## Comparison

| Approach | Convergence Speed | Complexity | SRv6 Required | Header Overhead |
|----------|:-----------------:|:----------:|:--------------:|:---------------:|
| **Local Delay** | Delayed (configurable) | Low | Yes (TI-LFA) | None |
| **Explicit Path** | Immediate | Medium | Yes (SIDs) | Temporary SRH |
| **Ordered FIB** | Slow (ordered) | High | No | None |

## Verification

=== "Cisco IOS-XR"

    ```cisco
    !! Verify micro-loop avoidance is enabled
    show isis microloop-avoidance status

    !! Show active micro-loop avoidance events
    show isis microloop-avoidance

    !! Verify TI-LFA is protecting during delay
    show isis fast-reroute ipv6 summary

    !! Monitor convergence with timestamps
    show isis convergence
    ```

=== "Juniper"

    ```junos
    show isis spf log
    show isis overview | match microloop
    ```

## Deployment Recommendations

1. **Enable TI-LFA first** — micro-loop avoidance depends on TI-LFA for traffic protection during the delay window
2. **Start with local delay** — simplest approach, 5000-10000ms is a safe default
3. **Tune the delay timer** — measure your network's worst-case convergence time; set the delay to 2x that value
4. **Test with controlled failures** — shut a link and verify no packet loss during the micro-loop window
5. **Monitor with telemetry** — track convergence events and micro-loop avoidance activations

## Further Reading

- [TI-LFA](https://srv6.md/topics/ti-lfa/) — Sub-50ms fast reroute (prerequisite for micro-loop avoidance)
- [Performance & Scaling](https://srv6.md/topics/performance-scaling/) — Convergence benchmarks
- [Telemetry](https://srv6.md/topics/telemetry/) — Monitoring convergence events
- [RFC 9855](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9855/) — TI-LFA Using Segment Routing

## References

1. [RFC 9855 - Topology Independent Fast Reroute Using Segment Routing](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9855/) - TI-LFA standard that enables micro-loop avoidance in SRv6 networks
2. [RFC 8333 - Micro-loop Prevention by Introducing a Local Convergence Delay](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8333/) - Defines the local delay mechanism for micro-loop prevention
3. [Cisco IOS-XR: Configure Microloop Avoidance](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/td/docs/iosxr/cisco8000/segment-routing/24xx/configuration/guide/b-segment-routing-cg-cisco8000-24xx/configuring-topology-independent-loop-free-alternate.html) - IOS-XR configuration guide for micro-loop avoidance with segment routing

# SRv6 in CLOS Data Centers: Deterministic Load Balancing

URL: https://srv6.md/topics/clos-glb/
Path: topics/clos-glb.md
Summary: SRv6 in CLOS data center fabrics: the ECMP hash-collision problem, deterministic path placement, global load balancing with flowlets, and SRv6 vs VXLAN.

# CLOS Fabrics & Load Balancing

Modern data center networks use **CLOS (Spine-Leaf)** topologies with multiple equal-cost paths. SRv6 provides deterministic traffic placement across these paths, solving the fundamental limitations of traditional ECMP hashing.

## CLOS Topology Refresher

A CLOS fabric provides full bisectional bandwidth between any two leaf switches through multiple spine switches:

```mermaid
graph TB
    S1[Spine 1] --- L1[Leaf 1]
    S1 --- L2[Leaf 2]
    S1 --- L3[Leaf 3]
    S1 --- L4[Leaf 4]
    S2[Spine 2] --- L1
    S2 --- L2
    S2 --- L3
    S2 --- L4
    S3[Spine 3] --- L1
    S3 --- L2
    S3 --- L3
    S3 --- L4
```

## The ECMP Problem

Traditional ECMP (Equal-Cost Multi-Path) uses a hash of packet headers (5-tuple) to select a path. This works well for diverse traffic, but fails with:

- **Elephant flows** — large, long-lived flows that saturate a single path
- **Synchronized workloads** — AI/ML training where thousands of flows start and end simultaneously
- **Hash collisions** — multiple flows hashing to the same spine, causing congestion while other spines are idle
- **Hash polarization** — similar hash results at multiple layers of the fabric

## SRv6 Deterministic Path Placement

Instead of relying on hashing, SRv6 allows the **source** (host, NIC, or controller) to explicitly choose which spine each flow traverses:

```
Traditional ECMP:
  Packet → Hash(5-tuple) → Spine selection    (probabilistic)

SRv6 Path Placement:
  Packet → SRv6 SID(Spine-N) → Spine selection  (deterministic)
```

Each spine is assigned an SRv6 uSID. The source encapsulates the packet with the desired spine's SID, guaranteeing the path.

### Benefits

| Aspect | ECMP | SRv6 Deterministic |
|--------|:----:|:------------------:|
| Path selection | Hash-based (probabilistic) | Explicit (deterministic) |
| Elephant flow handling | Poor (collisions) | Optimal (controlled placement) |
| Fabric utilization | 60-80% typical | Near 100% achievable |
| Application awareness | None | Source can control path |
| Flowlet support | Limited | Native via SID switching |

## Global Load Balancing (GLB) and Flowlets

### What are Flowlets?

A **flowlet** is a burst of packets within a flow, separated by idle gaps. Unlike flow-level load balancing (which pins an entire flow to one path), **flowlet-based** load balancing can reassign traffic to different paths between bursts without causing reordering.

```
Flow timeline:
  ████████──gap──████████──gap──████████──gap──████████
  Flowlet 1       Flowlet 2       Flowlet 3       Flowlet 4
  → Spine 1       → Spine 2       → Spine 3       → Spine 1
```

### GLB with SRv6

Global Load Balancing (GLB) uses SRv6 to steer flowlets across different spines:

1. **Monitor** fabric link utilization or congestion signals
2. **Assign** each new flowlet to the least-loaded spine via SRv6 SID
3. **Reroute** between flowlet gaps — no packet reordering

This is especially powerful for **AI training** workloads where collective operations (AllReduce, AllGather) create predictable traffic bursts with natural gaps.

## BGP in CLOS + SRv6

BGP is the standard routing protocol for CLOS fabrics (replacing OSPF/IS-IS in many DC deployments). With SRv6:

### eBGP Underlay

Each leaf-spine link runs an eBGP session (each switch has its own ASN or uses BGP unnumbered):

```
Leaf ASN 65001 ──eBGP── Spine ASN 65100
Leaf ASN 65002 ──eBGP── Spine ASN 65100
```

### SRv6 Locator Advertisement

Each switch advertises its SRv6 locator via BGP, making SRv6 SIDs reachable across the fabric.

### Overlay Services

BGP EVPN over SRv6 provides:

- **L2 bridging** across the fabric (VXLAN replacement)
- **L3 routing** between VRFs
- **Distributed anycast gateway** at every leaf

## SRv6 vs VXLAN in Data Centers

| Aspect | VXLAN + ECMP | SRv6 uSID |
|--------|:------------:|:----------:|
| Encapsulation | UDP/VXLAN | IPv6 + SRH (or just DA with uSID) |
| Path control | Hash-based only | Deterministic or hash-based |
| TE capability | None | Full SR Policy support |
| Overhead | 50 bytes | 40 bytes (no SRH) or 56+ bytes (with SRH) |
| Flowlet support | Limited | Native via SID update between bursts |
| Standards | RFC 7348 | RFC 8986, RFC 9800 |

## Further Reading

- [AI/ML Training Networks](https://srv6.md/use-cases/ai-networking/) - SRv6 for GPU cluster fabrics
- [SRv6 AI Fabric Design](https://srv6.md/ai/ai-fabric-design/) - uSID addressing and static tables for multi-plane GPU fabrics
- [BGP Overlay Services](https://srv6.md/topics/bgp-overlay-services/) - EVPN and L3VPN over SRv6
- [uSID / SRv6 Compression](https://srv6.md/topics/usid-compression/) - Efficient path encoding
- [Traffic Engineering](https://srv6.md/use-cases/traffic-engineering/) - SR Policies

## References

1. [RFC 7938 - Use of BGP for Routing in Large-Scale Data Centers](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc7938/) - Defines BGP as the routing protocol for CLOS DC fabrics
2. [RFC 8986 - SRv6 Network Programming](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8986/) - SRv6 behaviors used for path placement in DC fabrics
3. [draft-filsfils-srv6ops-srv6-ai-backend](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-filsfils-srv6ops-srv6-ai-backend/) - SRv6 deterministic path placement for AI backend networks
4. [RFC 9800 - Compressed SRv6 Segment List Encoding](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9800/) - uSID compression enabling efficient spine selection

# EVPN Multihoming Explained: ESI, DF Election, Aliasing, SRv6

URL: https://srv6.md/topics/evpn-multihoming/
Path: topics/evpn-multihoming.md
Summary: EVPN multihoming (EVPN-MH) explained: ESI types, all-active vs single-active, DF election (modulo, HRW, preference), aliasing, mass withdrawal and split-horizon over MPLS and SRv6.

# EVPN Multihoming

**EVPN multihoming** (often shortened to EVPN-MH or EVPN multi-homing) lets a customer device — a switch, router, server or access node — attach to **two or more PE routers** over a single logical link, with the PEs coordinating through BGP instead of a proprietary MC-LAG control channel. It is defined in [RFC 7432](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7432) (the EVPN base specification) and refined by [RFC 8584](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8584) (DF election framework). [RFC 9252](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9252/) and [RFC 9819](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9819/) carry the same machinery over SRv6.

This page covers the generic mechanisms first — they are identical whether the core runs MPLS, VXLAN or SRv6 — and then the parts that change with an SRv6 data plane.

```mermaid
graph LR
    CE[CE<br/>LAG with 2 member links] ---|ES 1| PE1[PE1]
    CE ---|ES 1| PE2[PE2]
    PE1 <--> CORE((MPLS / SRv6 core))
    PE2 <--> CORE
    CORE <--> PE3[PE3 remote]
    PE3 --- RCE[Remote CE]
```

## Ethernet Segment and ESI

An **Ethernet Segment (ES)** is the set of links that connect one customer site to several PEs. From the CE's point of view it is usually a single LACP bundle; each PE sees one member link. Every PE attached to the segment configures the same **Ethernet Segment Identifier (ESI)**.

The ESI is **10 octets**: a 1-octet type followed by a 9-octet value ([RFC 7432 §5](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7432#section-5)). Two values are reserved: all zeros means "single-homed, no ES", and all `FF` (MAX-ESI) is reserved.

| Type | Value is built from | Typical use |
|:----:|---------------------|-------------|
| **0** | 9 octets configured by the operator | Most common; you pick a unique value per segment |
| **1** | CE LACP system MAC (6) + port key (2) + 0 | Auto-derived from LACP when the CE runs LACP |
| **2** | IST root bridge MAC (6) + root bridge priority (2) + 0 | CE is a bridged LAN running MSTP; the PE learns the values from BPDUs |
| **3** | System MAC (6) + local discriminator (3) | Auto-generated by the PE from a MAC |
| **4** | Router ID (4) + local discriminator (4) + 0 | Auto-generated from the PE/CE router ID |
| **5** | AS number (4) + local discriminator (4) + 0 | Auto-generated from an ASN |

!!! tip "Type 0 vs auto-derived ESIs"
    Type 0 is explicit and portable between vendors. Auto-derived types save configuration on large access networks, but check what your vendor actually derives from: RFC 7432 Type 1 uses the **CE's** LACP system MAC and port key, while Junos `auto-derive lacp` builds the ESI from the **PE's own** LACP system ID and admin key (which must then be identical on every PE). Either way, all PEs on an all-active LAG must present the same LACP system ID to the CE, or the CE will not bundle the links.

## EVPN Routes Used for Multihoming

| Route | Name | Multihoming role |
|-------|------|------------------|
| **Type 4** | Ethernet Segment | Discovery of the other PEs on the same ES and **DF election**. Carries the ES-Import Route Target (auto-derived from the ESI value for types 1–3), so only PEs on that ES import it |
| **Type 1** | Ethernet A-D **per ES** | Advertises the redundancy mode (single-active flag in the ESI Label extended community) and the split-horizon label/argument; withdrawing it is the **mass withdrawal** signal |
| **Type 1** | Ethernet A-D **per EVI** | Advertised per service instance; lets remote PEs build **aliasing** (all-active) or **backup paths** (single-active) |
| **Type 2** | MAC/IP Advertisement | MAC and ARP/ND bindings; synced between PEs on the same ES |
| **Type 3** | Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag | BUM delivery; in SRv6 also carries the End.DT2M SID |
| **Type 5** | IP Prefix ([RFC 9136](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9136)) | Routed prefixes, used by EVPN L3 multihoming |

## All-Active vs Single-Active

| | **All-active** | **Single-active** |
|--|----------------|-------------------|
| Who forwards known unicast | Every PE on the ES | Only the DF for that VLAN/EVI |
| CE side | One LAG across the PEs | Separate links or LAG with standby members; the non-DF blocks its port for that service |
| Remote PE behavior | ECMP to all PEs on the ES (**aliasing**) | Primary path to the DF, pre-programmed **backup path** to the non-DF |
| BUM toward the CE | Only the DF sends | Only the DF sends |
| Loop prevention needed | **Split-horizon** filtering (BUM received from the ES must not be sent back into it) | Not for the CE (the non-DF does not forward) |
| Typical use | Data center leaf pairs, access aggregation, bandwidth | Hand-offs to devices that cannot run a cross-chassis LAG, strict per-VLAN active/standby |

A third mode, **port-active** ([RFC 9786](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9786), June 2025), elects one PE per interface rather than per VLAN — a drop-in replacement for MC-LAG active/standby. The DF election for port-active can use any of the algorithms below.

## Designated Forwarder (DF) Election

When the CE floods a broadcast or unknown-unicast frame, every PE on the ES would deliver remote BUM copies back to it. The **DF** is the one PE per  that sends BUM toward the CE; the others drop it.

PEs learn each other through Type 4 routes, wait for the **DF election timer** (3 seconds by default) so all routes arrive, then run the election.

| Algorithm | Defined in | How it picks the DF | Trade-off |
|-----------|-----------|---------------------|-----------|
| **Modulo / service carving** (default) | RFC 7432 §8.5 | Sort PE IPs ascending (index 0..N-1); DF for VLAN *V* is index `V mod N` | Simple, but when a PE joins or leaves, almost every VLAN moves |
| **HRW** (Highest Random Weight) | RFC 8584 §3 | Each PE computes a hash weight of (VLAN, ESI, PE address); highest wins, ties go to the lowest IP | Only the VLANs of the failed/added PE move; even spread with sparse VLAN IDs |
| **Preference-based** | [RFC 9785](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9785) (June 2025) | Operator sets a 2-octet preference per PE per ES; highest (DF Alg 2) or lowest (DF Alg 3) wins; the **D** (Don't Preempt) bit makes it non-revertive | Deterministic primary/backup per ES; the norm for single-active designs |
| **AC-influenced (AC-DF)** | RFC 8584 | Any of the above, but a PE whose attachment circuit is down for that EVI is excluded | Avoids electing a DF that cannot actually forward |

RFC 8584 also introduced the **DF Election extended community** on the Type 4 route: a 5-bit algorithm field (0 = modulo, 1 = HRW, 2/3 = highest/lowest preference) and a capability bitmap (D, AC-DF, …). If the PEs on a segment disagree, they all fall back to modulo. Vendor support varies: Cisco IOS-XR and Junos expose modulo and preference-based election in configuration, so check the release notes before designing around HRW.

```text
Modulo example: ES with PE1 (192.0.2.1) and PE2 (192.0.2.2), N = 2
  Ordered list: [PE1, PE2]
  VLAN 100 → 100 mod 2 = 0 → PE1 is DF
  VLAN 101 → 101 mod 2 = 1 → PE2 is DF
  If you only use even VLANs, PE1 is DF for everything — HRW avoids this.
```

## Aliasing and Backup Path

A MAC address behind a multihomed CE may only be learned (and advertised in a Type 2 route) by **one** of the PEs — the one whose LAG member the CE hashed that flow onto. Without help, remote PEs would send all traffic for that MAC to that single PE.

**Aliasing** fixes this: each PE advertises an Ethernet A-D **per EVI** route for the ES. A remote PE that sees a Type 2 route with a non-zero ESI looks up every PE that advertised A-D per EVI for that ESI and load-balances across all of them, even the ones that never learned the MAC.

In **single-active** mode the same routes provide a **backup path**: the remote PE installs the DF as primary and the other PE as a pre-programmed backup, ready for fast switchover.

## Mass Withdrawal

If PE1 loses its link to a CE with 10 000 MACs, withdrawing 10 000 Type 2 routes takes time. Instead, PE1 withdraws a single **Ethernet A-D per ES** route. Every remote PE immediately removes PE1 from the next-hop set of *all* MACs associated with that ESI — a prefix-independent convergence step — and the individual Type 2 withdrawals follow in the background.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant CE
    participant PE1
    participant PE2
    participant PE3 as PE3 (remote)

    Note over CE,PE1: Link CE–PE1 fails
    PE1->>PE3: Withdraw Ethernet A-D per ES (ESI 1)
    PE3->>PE3: Remove PE1 from every MAC/IP with ESI 1
    Note over PE3: All flows now go to PE2 only
    PE1->>PE3: (later) Withdraw individual Type 2 routes
```

## Split-Horizon Filtering

In all-active mode, a BUM frame from the CE arrives at PE1, which floods it to every PE in the EVI — including PE2, which is attached to the **same** ES. If PE2 is the DF, it would send the frame straight back to the CE, creating a loop or duplicate. Split-horizon stops this: the receiving PE must know *which ES the frame came from* and skip that ES.

How the "came from" information is carried depends on the data plane:

| Data plane | Mechanism | Defined in |
|------------|-----------|------------|
| **MPLS** | **ESI label**: each PE advertises a label in its A-D per ES route; the ingress PE pushes the egress PE's ESI label beneath the EVPN label on BUM sent to it. The egress PE sees the label and does not forward onto that ES | RFC 7432 §8.3 |
| **VXLAN / NVO** | **Local bias**: no label space for an ESI label, so the egress PE uses the outer source IP to recognize a peer on the same ES; the ingress PE always floods locally to its own ESs regardless of DF state | RFC 8365 §8.3.1 |
| **SRv6** | **ESI-filtering argument (Arg.FE2)** carried in the argument bits of the egress PE's **End.DT2M** SID — the SRv6 equivalent of the ESI label. Local bias is also allowed | RFC 8986 §4.12, RFC 9252 §6.1.1/§6.3, RFC 9819 |

[RFC 9746](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9746) (March 2025) lets PEs signal which method they use, with a Split-Horizon Type field in the ESI Label extended community: MPLS defaults to ESI-label filtering, VXLAN to local bias, and **SRv6 defaults to ESI filtering but supports both**. Local bias only works with all-active redundancy.

## EVPN Multihoming over SRv6

SRv6 has no label stack to push an ESI label onto, so the egress PE's local ES identifier travels as an **argument** inside the SID itself:

1. Each PE allocates an **End.DT2M** SID per bridge domain for BUM traffic and advertises its `LOC:FUNC` part in the **Type 3 (IMET)** route.
2. For each local ES it allocates an **Arg.FE2** value and advertises it in the **Type 1 A-D per ES** route (SRv6 L2 Service TLV).
3. When PE1 floods BUM that it received from ES 1 to PE2, it combines PE2's End.DT2M `LOC:FUNC` with PE2's Arg.FE2 for ES 1 into the destination address.
4. PE2 executes End.DT2M: it decapsulates and floods into the bridge domain, **excluding** the interfaces of the ES identified by the argument.

```text
PE2 Type 3 route:  End.DT2M LOC:FUNC = fc00:0:2:e002::   SID structure 32/16/16, AL 16
PE2 Type 1 route:  Arg.FE2 for ES 1  = 0x00a1             AL 16
PE1 → PE2, BUM received from ES 1:
    argument inserted at offset 32+16+16 = 64 bits
    DA = fc00:0:2:e002:a1::
PE2: End.DT2M with argument 0x00a1 → flood to every AC in the bridge domain except ES 1
```

!!! warning "Why RFC 9819 exists"
    RFC 9252 said the ingress PE SHOULD bitwise-OR the Type 3 SID and the Type 1 argument. That only works when both routes use the same SID structure; interop testing found implementations disagreeing. [RFC 9819](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9819/) (July 2025) replaces the OR with an explicit rule: insert the argument at offset LBL + LNL + FL taken from the **Type 3** route's SID Structure, and stop forwarding BUM from that ES if the two routes announce different argument lengths. If you mix vendors on an SRv6 EVPN all-active segment, check RFC 9819 support first.

Known unicast does not need split-horizon. Remote PEs use **End.DT2U** (bridge-table lookup) or **End.DX2** (cross-connect, for EVPN-VPWS) SIDs from the Type 1 per-EVI and Type 2 routes, and aliasing simply becomes ECMP across the SRv6 SIDs of all PEs on the ES. With [uSID](https://srv6.md/topics/usid-compression/) these service SIDs are typically uDT2U/uDT2M micro-SIDs on the PE's locator.

The underlay contributes too: [TI-LFA](https://srv6.md/topics/ti-lfa/) protects the core paths between PEs, while mass withdrawal and aliasing protect the attachment circuit — the two mechanisms are complementary.

## EVPN L3 Multihoming (Routed CE)

When the CE is a router and the service is an L3VPN, the same ES concepts apply to a routed hand-off. [draft-ietf-bess-evpn-l3mh-proto](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-bess-evpn-l3mh-proto/) specifies **EVPN L3 multihoming**:

1. CE connects to PE1 and PE2 via an Ethernet Segment (same ESI on both PEs)
2. PEs discover each other via Type 4 routes and elect a DF
3. ARP/ND entries learned by one PE are synced to the other with Type 2 routes, so either PE can route to the CE immediately
4. Prefixes are advertised to remote PEs as Type 5 (or VPNv4/VPNv6) routes with SRv6 **End.DT4/End.DT6/End.DT46** service SIDs
5. Remote PEs ECMP across both PEs; on PE or link failure, the Type 1 per-ES withdrawal triggers fast reconvergence

| Aspect | L2 multihoming (EVPN) | L3 multihoming (EVPN L3MH) |
|--------|----------------------|---------------------------|
| **Service type** | L2VPN / bridging | L3VPN / routing |
| **CE attachment** | Bridge domain | VRF / routed interface |
| **MAC learning** | Required | Only for ARP/ND sync |
| **Split-horizon** | Per ES (ESI label / Arg.FE2) | Not needed for routed traffic |
| **Prefix advertisement** | Type 2 (MAC/IP) | Type 5 (IP Prefix) + Type 2 (ARP/ND sync) |
| **SRv6 service SIDs** | End.DT2U, End.DT2M, End.DX2 | End.DT4, End.DT6, End.DT46 |

!!! note "Interoperability"
    EVPN L3 multihoming has been demonstrated in multi-vendor interoperability tests (EANTC) with Cisco and Nokia using both SRv6 and SR-MPLS underlays.

## EVPN Multihoming vs MC-LAG

| | EVPN multihoming | MC-LAG / MLAG |
|--|------------------|---------------|
| Control plane | Standard BGP (RFC 7432) | Vendor-specific (ICCP, peer-link) |
| Number of PEs | 2 or more | Usually exactly 2 |
| Peer link between PEs | Not required | Usually required |
| Multivendor PE pair | Possible | No |
| Works across a routed core (MPLS, VXLAN, SRv6) | Yes | Typically same site only |

## Configuration Examples

Both PEs on the segment get the same ESI and redundancy mode. The examples use the type 0 ESI `00:11:22:33:44:55:66:77:88:99` with preference-based DF election (PE1 preferred).

=== "Cisco IOS-XR"

    ```cisco
    !! PE1 (use weight 50 on PE2)
    interface Bundle-Ether10
     lacp system mac 0011.2233.4455
    !
    evpn
     interface Bundle-Ether10
      ethernet-segment
       identifier type 0 11.22.33.44.55.66.77.88.99
       !! all-active is the default; alternatives:
       !! load-balancing-mode single-active | port-active
       service-carving preference-based
        weight 100
      !
     !
     !! SRv6: EVPN services take SIDs from this locator
     segment-routing srv6
      locator MAIN
     !
    !
    ```

=== "Junos"

    ```junos
    # PE1 (use preference value 50 on PE2)
    set interfaces ae0 esi 00:11:22:33:44:55:66:77:88:99
    set interfaces ae0 esi all-active
    set interfaces ae0 esi df-election-type preference value 100
    # identical LACP system ID on every PE of the segment
    set interfaces ae0 aggregated-ether-options lacp active
    set interfaces ae0 aggregated-ether-options lacp system-id 00:11:22:33:44:55
    ```

!!! note "ESI notation"
    IOS-XR takes the 9-octet **value** after `type 0`; Junos takes all 10 octets, and a manually configured Junos ESI must start with `00` (type 0). The two lines above describe the same segment. IOS-XR locator precedence for EVPN SRv6 SIDs is per-service, then per-EVI (`evi N segment-routing srv6` → `locator`), then the global `evpn segment-routing srv6 locator`.

## Common Pitfalls

- **ESI mismatch**: a typo in one PE's ESI silently turns an all-active segment into two single-homed sites — the CE sees duplicate BUM and MAC flaps.
- **LACP system ID**: for an all-active LAG, every PE must present the same LACP system ID and key to the CE.
- **Mixed DF algorithms**: PEs that advertise different DF algorithms fall back to modulo; check the DF Election extended community on the Type 4 routes.
- **Core isolation**: if a PE loses all core connectivity but keeps its CE link up, the CE keeps hashing traffic into a black hole. Most implementations bring the access interface down on core isolation — enable it.
- **SRv6 argument length**: on SRv6, the End.DT2M argument length must match between Type 1 and Type 3 routes (RFC 9819); mismatches stop BUM from that segment.

- [VPN Services](https://srv6.md/use-cases/vpn-services/) — SRv6 VPN use cases

# SRv6 QoS: Traffic Class, DSCP and Per-Policy QoS

URL: https://srv6.md/topics/qos/
Path: topics/qos.md
Summary: Quality of Service mechanisms in SRv6 — traffic class, DSCP, Flex-Algo constraints, and per-policy QoS

# QoS & Traffic Classification

SRv6 inherits IPv6's native QoS capabilities and extends them with segment routing-specific mechanisms. Together, they provide end-to-end traffic differentiation without the complexity of MPLS EXP bits, QoS-to-label mappings, or per-hop behavior configurations at every transit node.

## IPv6 Traffic Class Field

Every SRv6 packet carries QoS information in the IPv6 header's **Traffic Class** (TC) field — an 8-bit field composed of:

```
  0   1   2   3   4   5   6   7
+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+
|        DSCP (6 bits)      |ECN|
+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+
```

| Component | Bits | Purpose |
|-----------|------|---------|
| **DSCP** | 6 | Differentiated Services Code Point — determines per-hop behavior (PHB) |
| **ECN** | 2 | Explicit Congestion Notification |

### Key advantage over MPLS

In MPLS, QoS relies on the 3-bit EXP field (8 possible values). SRv6 uses the full 6-bit DSCP (64 possible values), eliminating the need for complex EXP-to-DSCP remapping at domain boundaries.

| Feature | MPLS | SRv6 |
|---------|------|------|
| QoS bits available | 3 (EXP) | 6 (DSCP) |
| Possible classes | 8 | 64 |
| Remapping at boundaries | Required | Not needed |
| End-to-end consistency | Difficult | Native |

## DSCP Preservation

When a PE encapsulates a packet into SRv6, the original DSCP value can be:

1. **Copied** from the inner packet to the outer IPv6 header (uniform mode)
2. **Set explicitly** based on policy (pipe mode)
3. **Mapped** from inner DSCP to a different outer DSCP

### Uniform mode

The inner packet's DSCP is copied to the outer SRv6 header. Transit nodes apply QoS based on the outer header. At decapsulation, the inner DSCP is preserved.

```
Inner packet:  DSCP = AF41
                ↓ copy
Outer SRv6:    TC = AF41 → transit nodes honor AF41
                ↓ decap
Egress:        DSCP = AF41 (preserved)
```

### Pipe mode

The outer DSCP is set independently of the inner packet. This allows the SRv6 domain to apply its own QoS policy without affecting the customer's markings.

## Flex-Algorithm for QoS-Aware Paths

[Flex-Algorithm](https://srv6.md/topics/flex-algorithm/) enables **constraint-based path computation** that directly serves QoS objectives:

| Flex-Algo ID | Constraint | QoS Use Case |
|-------------|------------|--------------|
| 128 | Minimum latency | Real-time voice, gaming |
| 129 | Maximum bandwidth | Video streaming, bulk transfers |
| 130 | Avoid specific links | Regulatory, compliance |
| 131 | Latency + bandwidth | Premium SLA services |

### How it works

1. Links are annotated with metrics (latency, bandwidth, affinity) via IS-IS/OSPF
2. Each Flex-Algo defines a constraint (e.g., "minimize latency")
3. Nodes compute a separate topology per Flex-Algo
4. SRv6 SIDs are allocated per Flex-Algo — traffic steered to the appropriate SID automatically follows the constrained path

```mermaid
graph LR
    PE1[PE1] -->|Algo 128: Low Latency| P1[P1] -->|10ms| PE2[PE2]
    PE1 -->|Algo 129: High BW| P2[P2] -->|100Gbps| PE2
```

This replaces traditional RSVP-TE bandwidth reservations with a simpler, IGP-based approach.

## SR Policy QoS

[SR Policies](https://srv6.md/use-cases/traffic-engineering/) (SRv6-TE) can enforce QoS at the policy level:

### Per-policy DSCP marking

An SR Policy can set or remark the DSCP of traffic entering the policy:

| Policy | Color | DSCP Action |
|--------|-------|-------------|
| Gold SLA | 100 | Mark EF |
| Silver SLA | 200 | Mark AF31 |
| Best Effort | 300 | Mark BE |

### Weighted ECMP across candidate paths

An SR Policy can have multiple candidate paths with different weights, enabling proportional traffic distribution:

```
SR Policy to PE2:
  Candidate Path 1 (low-latency):  weight 30%
  Candidate Path 2 (high-capacity): weight 70%
```

## Network Slicing with QoS

SRv6 network slicing combines Flex-Algo with QoS to create isolated virtual networks, each with guaranteed performance characteristics:

| Slice | Flex-Algo | DSCP Range | SLA |
|-------|-----------|------------|-----|
| **5G URLLC** | 128 | EF, AF41 |  1 Gbps throughput |
| **Enterprise VPN** | 130 | AF31-AF33 | 99.99% availability |
| **Best Effort** | 0 (default) | BE | No guarantees |

Each slice operates on its own topology with dedicated SRv6 SIDs, ensuring **hard isolation** between traffic classes.

## QoS at SRv6 Endpoints

### End.DT4 / End.DT6 (VPN decapsulation)

At the egress PE, the SRv6 endpoint behavior decapsulates the packet and routes it into the VRF. The inner packet's DSCP is preserved, ensuring end-to-end QoS consistency.

### End.B6.Encaps (binding SID)

When a binding SID triggers re-encapsulation, the QoS policy can dictate how the new outer header's TC field is set — enabling QoS policy changes at domain boundaries without touching the inner packet.

## Comparison with MPLS QoS

| Aspect | MPLS QoS | SRv6 QoS |
|--------|----------|----------|
| **Classification bits** | 3-bit EXP (8 classes) | 6-bit DSCP (64 classes) |
| **Boundary remapping** | EXP ↔ DSCP at every boundary | Not needed — DSCP is native |
| **Path constraints** | RSVP-TE bandwidth reservations | Flex-Algo (IGP-based, no signaling) |
| **Per-hop config** | Required at every P node | Only at PE (transit is implicit) |
| **Network slicing** | Complex (VRF + TE tunnel per slice) | Native (Flex-Algo + SID per slice) |
| **Scalability** | TE tunnels = state at every hop | Stateless (source-routed) |

## Further Reading

- [Flex-Algorithm](https://srv6.md/topics/flex-algorithm/) — Constraint-based path computation
- [Network Slicing](https://srv6.md/use-cases/network-slicing/) — End-to-end slicing combining Flex-Algo + QoS + color steering
- [Traffic Engineering](https://srv6.md/use-cases/traffic-engineering/) — SR Policies and path control
- [5G Transport](https://srv6.md/use-cases/5g-transport/) — Network slicing for mobile
- [Performance & Scaling](https://srv6.md/topics/performance-scaling/) — MTU and encapsulation overhead
- [SRv6 vs SR-MPLS](https://srv6.md/topics/srv6-vs-sr-mpls/) — Comparison including QoS differences

## References

1. [RFC 2474](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc2474/) — Definition of the Differentiated Services Field in the IPv4 and IPv6 Headers
2. [RFC 8986](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8986/) — SRv6 Network Programming
3. [RFC 9256](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9256/) — Segment Routing Policy Architecture
4. [RFC 9350](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9350/) — IGP Flexible Algorithm
