# RFC 9514 Explained: BGP-LS Extensions for SRv6

URL: https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9514/
Path: rfcs/rfc9514.md
Summary: RFC 9514 explained in plain language: BGP-LS Extensions for SRv6. What it defines, how it works and how it fits into SRv6 networks.

# RFC 9514 - Border Gateway Protocol - Link State (BGP-LS) Extensions for SRv6

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Title** | Border Gateway Protocol - Link State (BGP-LS) Extensions for Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) |
| **Authors** | G. Dawra, C. Filsfils, K. Talaulikar, M. Chen, D. Bernier, B. Decraene |
| **Date** | December 2023 |
| **Status** | Proposed Standard |
| **Link** | [datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9514](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9514/) |

## Summary

RFC 9514 defines extensions to the Border Gateway Protocol - Link State (BGP-LS) for carrying SRv6 information. BGP-LS (RFC 7752, updated by RFC 9552) is used to export link-state topology and traffic engineering information from IGP domains to external consumers such as SDN controllers and Path Computation Elements (PCEs). This RFC extends BGP-LS to include SRv6-specific attributes.

The extensions enable a centralized controller to learn the complete SRv6 topology of the network, including SRv6 capabilities, locators, End SIDs, adjacency SIDs (End.X), and the SID structure. With this information, a controller can compute SRv6 paths and program SR Policies without needing to participate in the IGP directly.

This is a critical building block for SDN-based SRv6 deployments where a PCE or SDN controller computes paths centrally and distributes them via PCEP or BGP SR Policy. The BGP-LS SRv6 extensions ensure the controller has a complete and accurate view of the SRv6 data plane.

## Key Sections

| Section | Topic | Description |
|---------|-------|-------------|
| 3 | SRv6 Capabilities | Node-level SRv6 support advertisement via BGP-LS |
| 4 | SRv6 Locator | Prefix NLRI attribute carrying locator and algorithm |
| 5 | SRv6 End SID | BGP-LS attribute TLV for SRv6 endpoint behaviors |
| 6 | SRv6 Adjacency SID (End.X) | BGP-LS link attribute for per-adjacency SRv6 SIDs |
| 7 | SRv6 SID Structure | TLV describing the LOC:FUNC:ARG bit layout |

## BGP-LS SRv6 Attribute TLVs

| TLV | Code Point | BGP-LS Attribute | Maps From (IGP) |
|-----|-----------|-----------------|-----------------|
| **SRv6 Capabilities** | 1106 | Node Attribute | IS-IS / OSPFv3 SRv6 Capabilities |
| **SRv6 Locator** | 1162 | Prefix Attribute | IS-IS SRv6 Locator TLV / OSPFv3 SRv6 Locator TLV |
| **SRv6 End SID** | 1163 | Prefix Attribute | IS-IS SRv6 End SID sub-TLV / OSPFv3 SRv6 End SID sub-TLV |
| **SRv6 SID Structure** | 1164 | Prefix/Link Attribute | IS-IS / OSPFv3 SRv6 SID Structure sub-TLV |
| **SRv6 End.X SID** | 1106 | Link Attribute | IS-IS SRv6 End.X SID sub-TLV / OSPFv3 SRv6 Adj SID sub-TLV |

## BGP-LS to IGP Mapping

| BGP-LS Component | IS-IS Source | OSPFv3 Source |
|-----------------|-------------|---------------|
| Node NLRI + SRv6 Caps | Router Capability TLV | Router Information LSA |
| Prefix NLRI + SRv6 Locator | SRv6 Locator TLV | SRv6 Locator TLV in E-Router-LSA |
| Prefix NLRI + SRv6 End SID | SRv6 End SID sub-TLV | SRv6 End SID sub-TLV |
| Link NLRI + SRv6 End.X SID | SRv6 End.X SID sub-TLV | SRv6 Adjacency SID sub-TLV |

## Use with SDN Controllers and PCE

```
+------------------+
|  SDN Controller  |     BGP-LS provides the SRv6 topology database
|  / PCE           |     to the controller, which then computes
+--------+---------+     paths and programs SR Policies via PCEP
         |                or BGP SR Policy.
    BGP-LS Session
         |
+--------+---------+
|   BGP-LS Speaker |     Collects IGP SRv6 data from IS-IS/OSPFv3
|   (Route Reflector)    and exports via BGP-LS to the controller.
+--------+---------+
         |
    IGP Domain (IS-IS or OSPFv3 with SRv6 extensions)
```

| Component | Role |
|-----------|------|
| **BGP-LS Speaker** | Collects SRv6 information from the IGP and exports it northbound |
| **SDN Controller / PCE** | Consumes the BGP-LS SRv6 topology to compute constrained paths |
| **PCEP / BGP SR Policy** | Southbound protocol to push computed SR Policies to headend routers |

!!! warning "Common Pitfalls"
    - BGP-LS SRv6 extensions only export information -- they do not program the data plane. A separate mechanism (PCEP, BGP SR Policy) is needed to install computed paths.
    - The BGP-LS speaker must participate in the IGP to learn SRv6 TLVs. If the IGP peering is misconfigured or the IGP does not carry SRv6 extensions, BGP-LS will have an incomplete view.
    - Ensure the BGP-LS speaker's IGP implementation supports the SRv6-specific TLVs from RFC 9352 (IS-IS) or RFC 9513 (OSPFv3). Older implementations may silently drop unknown TLVs.
    - The SRv6 SID Structure TLV is essential for the controller to correctly parse the LOC:FUNC:ARG boundaries. Missing SID Structure information can lead to incorrect path computation.
    - Multi-domain deployments require BGP-LS from each domain. The controller must stitch cross-domain topology views to compute end-to-end SRv6 paths.

## Related Drafts & Updates

- [draft-ietf-idr-bgpls-srv6-ext](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-idr-bgpls-srv6-ext/) - Earlier draft lineage
- [RFC 9857](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9857/) - BGP-LS advertisement of SR Policies (formerly draft-ietf-idr-bgp-ls-sr-policy)

## Related

- [RFC 9513](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9513/) - OSPFv3 Extensions for SRv6
- [RFC 8402](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc8402/) - Segment Routing Architecture
- [RFC 9256](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9256/) - SR Policy Architecture

## References

1. [RFC 9514](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9514/) - BGP-LS Extensions for Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6)
2. [RFC 9552](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9552/) - Distribution of Link-State and TE Information Using BGP
3. [RFC 9352](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9352/) - IS-IS Extensions for Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6)
4. [RFC 9513](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9513/) - OSPFv3 Extensions for Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6)

# RFC 9603 Explained: PCEP Extensions for SRv6

URL: https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9603/
Path: rfcs/rfc9603.md
Summary: RFC 9603 explained in plain language: PCEP Extensions for IPv6 Segment Routing — SRv6 path setup type, SRv6-ERO and SRv6-RRO. What it defines, how it works and how it fits into SRv6 networks.

# RFC 9603 - PCEP Extensions for SRv6

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Title** | Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Extensions for IPv6 Segment Routing |
| **Authors** | C. Li (Ed.), P. Kaladharan, S. Sivabalan, M. Koldychev, Y. Zhu |
| **Date** | July 2024 |
| **Status** | Proposed Standard |
| **Link** | [datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9603](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9603/) |

## Summary

RFC 8664 taught PCEP to carry SR-MPLS paths. RFC 9603 does the same for **SRv6**, so a PCE can compute SRv6 paths and a stateful PCE can initiate, update, and receive reports for SRv6 SR Policy candidate paths on a headend (PCC).

The extension is small and reuses the existing PCEP messages unchanged. It adds a new **Path Setup Type (PST = 3)**, an **SRv6-PCE-CAPABILITY** sub-TLV exchanged in the OPEN message, and new **SRv6-ERO / SRv6-RRO** subobjects that carry 128-bit SIDs, optionally with the node/adjacency they belong to (the NAI), the endpoint behavior, and the SID structure.

## Key Sections

| Section | Topic | Description |
|---------|-------|-------------|
| 3 | Overview | How SRv6 fits on top of RFC 8664 procedures |
| 4.1 | OPEN Object | PST=3 and SRv6-PCE-CAPABILITY sub-TLV (with optional SRv6 MSDs) |
| 4.2 | RP/SRP Object | PATH-SETUP-TYPE TLV with PST=3 is mandatory for SRv6 messages |
| 4.3 | SRv6-ERO | SID, NAI, endpoint behavior, SID structure |
| 4.4 | SRv6-RRO | Reports the SID list actually applied by the PCC |
| 5 | Procedures | Capability exchange, ERO/RRO validation and error codes |

## What It Adds

| Element | Codepoint | Purpose |
|---------|-----------|---------|
| Path Setup Type | PST = 3 | "Path is set up using SRv6" |
| SRv6-PCE-CAPABILITY sub-TLV | Type 27 | Signals SRv6 support; PCC may add SRv6 MSD pairs and the N flag (can resolve NAI to SID) |
| SRv6-ERO subobject | Type 40 | One SRv6 segment of the computed path |
| SRv6-RRO subobject | Type 40 | One SRv6 segment of the path actually used |

## SRv6-ERO Subobject

| Field / Flag | Meaning |
|--------------|---------|
| **L** | Loose hop — PCC may expand or replace SIDs |
| **NT** | NAI type: 0 = none, 2 = IPv6 node ID, 4 = IPv6 adjacency, 6 = link-local adjacency |
| **S** | SID absent — PCC resolves it from the NAI |
| **F** | NAI absent |
| **T** | SID Structure present (LB, LN, Function, Argument lengths) |
| **V** | Verify the SID before use ([RFC 9256](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9256/) Section 5.1) |
| **Endpoint Behavior** | 16-bit [RFC 8986](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc8986/) behavior code (`0xFFFF` if unknown) |

An SRv6-ERO must carry a SID, an NAI, or both, and an ERO cannot mix SRv6-ERO with other subobject types.

## MSD Handling

A PCC may advertise its SRv6 Maximum SID Depths in the capability sub-TLV, but the PCE must consider the MSDs of **every node on the path**, not just the headend. If MSDs are available from IGP or [BGP-LS](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9514/), those take precedence, and the RFC recommends leaving them out of PCEP in that case. A PCC that receives a path exceeding its MSD returns a PCErr (Error-Type 10, value 40).

!!! warning "Common Pitfalls"
    - Every SRv6 PCEP message must carry PST=3 in the RP or SRP object; sending an SRv6-ERO without it, or without having exchanged the capability, triggers a PCErr (Type 19, value 19).
    - Advertising PST=3 without the SRv6-PCE-CAPABILITY sub-TLV closes the session.
    - Changing the PCC's advertised MSD requires tearing down and re-establishing the PCEP session.
    - The SID Structure is optional but useful: it lets the PCE validate SIDs against the operator's allocation plan.
    - RFC 9603 covers point-to-point SR Policies. Point-to-multipoint trees ([RFC 9960](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9960/)) use a separate draft.

## Related Drafts & Updates

| Document | Relationship | Description |
|----------|-------------|-------------|
| [RFC 8664](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8664/) | Extended by this RFC | PCEP extensions for SR-MPLS |
| [draft-ietf-pce-segment-routing-ipv6](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-pce-segment-routing-ipv6/) | Draft lineage | Draft that became RFC 9603 |
| [draft-ietf-pce-segment-routing-policy-cp](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-pce-segment-routing-policy-cp/) | Companion | PCEP extensions for SR Policy candidate paths |
| [draft-ietf-pce-sr-p2mp-policy](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-pce-sr-p2mp-policy/) | Companion | PCEP extensions for SR P2MP Policy |

# RFC 9830 Explained: Advertising SR Policies in BGP

URL: https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9830/
Path: rfcs/rfc9830.md
Summary: RFC 9830 explained: the BGP SR Policy SAFI (73) that lets controllers push SR Policy candidate paths to headends, with SRv6 Binding SIDs and SRv6 segment encoding.

# RFC 9830 - Advertising Segment Routing Policies in BGP

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Title** | Advertising Segment Routing Policies in BGP |
| **Authors** | S. Previdi, C. Filsfils, K. Talaulikar (Ed.), P. Mattes, D. Jain |
| **Date** | September 2025 |
| **Status** | Proposed Standard |
| **Updates** | RFC 9012 (Color Extended Community) |
| **Link** | [rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9830](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9830/) |

## Summary

RFC 9830 defines the **BGP SR Policy SAFI** (SAFI 73), the standard way for a controller, or an egress router, to push the candidate paths of an [SR Policy](https://srv6.md/topics/sr-policy/) to the headends that should instantiate them. It is the BGP counterpart of PCEP ([RFC 9603](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9603/)) for SR Policy provisioning, and it works for both SR-MPLS and SRv6.

BGP is only the transport. A headend runs normal BGP best-path selection, then hands the received candidate path to its **SR Policy Module (SRPM)**, which validates it, selects the active candidate path per the [SR Policy Architecture (RFC 9256)](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9256/), binds the Binding SID and programs forwarding. BGP itself never installs the policy and does not validate the meaning of the segment lists.

Its companion [RFC 9857](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9857/) closes the loop in the other direction: controllers push policies with this SAFI and read their operational state back through BGP-LS.

## Key Sections

| Section | Topic | Description |
|---------|-------|-------------|
| 2.1 | SR Policy SAFI NLRI | SAFI 73 with AFI 1 or 2; NLRI = Distinguisher + Color + Endpoint |
| 2.2 | Tunnel Encapsulation Attribute | The policy rides in Tunnel Type 15, "SR Policy" |
| 2.4 | SR Policy sub-TLVs | Preference, Binding SIDs, segment lists, ENLP, priority, names |
| 2.4.3 | SRv6 Binding SID | 16-octet SRv6 BSID with optional endpoint behavior and SID structure |
| 2.4.4 | Segment List and segments | Explicit paths, weights, segment types A (SR-MPLS) and B (SRv6) |
| 3 | Color Extended Community | Color-Only bits that control endpoint matching for steering |
| 4 | Advertisement and validation | Route Targets vs NO_ADVERTISE, usability, propagation rules |
| 5 | Error handling | Treat-as-withdraw for invalid NLRI, TLVs and sub-TLVs |

## The NLRI

| Field | Size | Meaning |
|-------|------|---------|
| **Distinguisher** | 4 octets | No semantic value; separates several candidate paths of one policy, or policies for different headends with the same Color and Endpoint |
| **Color** | 4 octets | Non-zero value that matches destination prefixes (via their Color Extended Community) to the policy |
| **Endpoint** | 4 or 16 octets | IPv4 or IPv6 endpoint; can be the null endpoint (0.0.0.0 or ::) |

The policy content travels in the Tunnel Encapsulation Attribute (type 23) with **Tunnel Type 15**. Only one SR Policy TLV is allowed per attribute.

## SR Policy Sub-TLVs

| Sub-TLV | Type | Notes |
|---------|:----:|-------|
| Preference | 12 | Candidate path preference used by the SRPM |
| Binding SID | 13 | Generic BSID (SR-MPLS label or SRv6 SID) |
| **SRv6 Binding SID** | **20** | 16-octet SID, flags S/I/B, optional endpoint behavior and SID structure; recommended over type 13 for SRv6 |
| Segment List | 128 | One explicit path; may repeat for multiple weighted paths |
| Weight | 9 | Inside a Segment List; zero is invalid |
| ENLP | 14 | Explicit NULL Label Policy (values 1–4) |
| Priority | 15 | Order in which policies are recomputed after a topology change |
| Candidate Path Name | 129 | Symbolic name of the candidate path |
| SR Policy Name | 130 | Symbolic name of the policy |

None of these sub-TLVs affect BGP best-path selection or how the route propagates.

## SRv6-Specific Pieces

| Element | Detail |
|---------|--------|
| **Segment Type B (type 13)** | One 16-octet SRv6 SID per segment |
| **Endpoint behavior and SID structure** | Optional on Type B segments and the SRv6 BSID: a 2-octet [RFC 8986](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc8986/) behavior codepoint (0xFFFF = opaque, headend decides) plus Locator Block / Locator Node / Function / Argument lengths, which must total 128 bits or less |
| **No mixing** | A segment list must not mix SR-MPLS and SRv6 segments |
| **More segment types** | Types C–K (including SRv6 SIDs expressed as node or adjacency addresses) are defined in the companion [RFC 9831](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9831/) |

## Who Gets the Policy: Route Targets vs NO_ADVERTISE

- An advertisement **SHOULD** carry Route Targets in IPv4-address format that identify the intended headends; a headend treats the update as usable only if one Route Target matches its BGP Identifier.
- Without a Route Target, the update **MUST** carry the NO_ADVERTISE community, which makes it usable by the receiving neighbor and never propagated further.
- SR Policy routes are not sent to EBGP neighbors by default, but they follow normal IBGP rules, so route reflectors can carry them.
- An update with unrecognized sub-TLVs should be treated as not usable; if an update becomes unusable, BGP removes the candidate path from the SRPM.

!!! warning "Common Pitfalls"
    - The Distinguisher is not a policy identifier. Two candidate paths of the **same** policy differ only by Distinguisher; the policy is Color + Endpoint (+ headend).
    - Forgetting both a matching Route Target and NO_ADVERTISE makes the update **invalid**, not just unusable, so it never reaches the SRPM.
    - Dynamic and composite candidate paths from RFC 9256 are out of scope; this SAFI carries **explicit** candidate paths.
    - SR Policies can expose sensitive topology. Keep SAFI 73 on dedicated sessions inside the trusted SR domain.

## Related Drafts & Updates

| Document | Relationship | Description |
|----------|-------------|-------------|
| [draft-ietf-idr-sr-policy-safi](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-idr-sr-policy-safi/) | Draft lineage | Draft that became RFC 9830 |
| [RFC 9831](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9831/) | Companion | Segment Type Extensions for BGP SR Policy (types C–K) |
| [RFC 9857](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9857/) | Complement | Reports SR Policy state back to controllers through BGP-LS |
| [RFC 9012](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9012/) | Updated | BGP Tunnel Encapsulation Attribute (Color Extended Community) |

## Related

- [SR Policy](https://srv6.md/topics/sr-policy/) - Candidate paths, Binding SIDs, color steering and ODN
- [Traffic Engineering](https://srv6.md/use-cases/traffic-engineering/) - SRv6 traffic engineering with SR Policies
- [RFC 9256](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9256/) - SR Policy Architecture
- [RFC 9603](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9603/) - PCEP Extensions for SRv6
- [RFC 9857](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9857/) - SR Policies in BGP-LS

## References

2. [RFC 9831](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9831) - Segment Type Extensions for BGP Segment Routing (SR) Policy
3. [RFC 9256](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9256) - Segment Routing Policy Architecture

# RFC 9857 Explained: SR Policies in BGP-LS

URL: https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9857/
Path: rfcs/rfc9857.md
Summary: Advertisement of Segment Routing Policies Using BGP-LS — reporting SR Policy candidate path state to controllers

# RFC 9857 - BGP-LS Advertisement of SR Policies

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Title** | Advertisement of Segment Routing Policies Using BGP - Link State |
| **Authors** | S. Previdi, K. Talaulikar (Ed.), J. Dong, H. Gredler, J. Tantsura |
| **Date** | October 2025 |
| **Status** | Proposed Standard |
| **Link** | [datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9857](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9857/) |

## Summary

[RFC 9514](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9514/) lets a controller learn SRv6 **topology** (locators, SIDs) through BGP-LS. RFC 9857 adds the other half: the **state of SR Policies** instantiated on headends. Each SR Policy candidate path — whether configured locally, pushed via PCEP, or pushed via the BGP SR Policy SAFI — can be reported with its Binding SID, state, constraints, and segment lists, for both SR-MPLS and SRv6.

This matters when the headend does not speak PCEP (management-based PCE), when a parent PCE needs a global view from child PCEs, or when a service-placement system or NMS needs to see which policies exist and whether they are up. It closes the loop for the BGP SR Policy SAFI ([RFC 9830](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9830/)): controllers push policies with BGP and read their operational state back with BGP-LS.

The BGP-LS producer can be the headend itself or a PCE relaying what its PCCs report.

## Key Sections

| Section | Topic | Description |
|---------|-------|-------------|
| 3 | SR Policy Candidate Path NLRI | New NLRI type 5 with Protocol-ID 9 ("Segment Routing") |
| 4 | Candidate Path Descriptor | Endpoint, color, originator, discriminator, protocol-origin |
| 5.1-5.2 | Binding SID TLVs | SR-MPLS BSID and SRv6 BSID with allocation/fallback flags |
| 5.3-5.5 | State and Names | Candidate path state, policy name, candidate path name |
| 5.6 | Constraints | Affinity, SRLG, bandwidth, disjointness, bidirectional, metric |
| 5.7 | Segment Lists | Per-segment encoding (types A-K), metrics, bandwidth, identifiers |

## New Codepoints

| Type | Name |
|------|------|
| NLRI 5 | SR Policy Candidate Path NLRI |
| Protocol-ID 9 | Segment Routing |
| TLV 554 | SR Policy Candidate Path Descriptor |
| TLV 1201 | SR Binding SID (SR-MPLS) |
| TLV 1202 | SR Candidate Path State |
| TLV 1203 / 1213 | SR Candidate Path Name / SR Policy Name |
| TLV 1204 | SR Candidate Path Constraints (sub-TLVs 1208-1211, 1214, 1215) |
| TLV 1205 / 1206 | SR Segment List / SR Segment |
| TLV 1207 / 1216 / 1217 | Segment List Metric / Bandwidth / Identifier |
| TLV 1212 | **SRv6 Binding SID** |

## SRv6-Specific Pieces

| Element | Detail |
|---------|--------|
| **SRv6 Binding SID TLV (1212)** | 128-bit BSID plus the *specified* BSID; flags B (allocated), U (specified BSID unavailable), F (fell back to dynamic) |
| **SRv6 segment types** | Type B (SRv6 SID), Type I (End SID by node address), Types J/K (End.X SID by adjacency, global or link-local) |
| **Behavior and structure** | The RFC 9514 SRv6 Endpoint Behavior TLV (1250) and SID Structure TLV (1252) can be attached as sub-TLVs to a BSID or a segment |

## Protocol-Origin Values

| Value | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| 1 / 2 / 3 | PCEP / BGP SR Policy / Configuration (CLI, YANG, NETCONF) — reported by the headend |
| 10 / 20 / 30 | Same origins, reported by a PCE acting as the BGP-LS producer |

!!! warning "Common Pitfalls"
    - The NLRI reports state at **candidate-path** granularity; composite candidate paths are out of scope.
    - Large policy counts produce many BGP-LS updates. Check whether the platform lets you filter which policies are exported.
    - The Local Node Descriptor identifies the **headend**, even when a PCE is the producer — do not mistake it for the BGP-LS speaker.
    - Other TE path types (e.g., RSVP-TE LSPs) are handled by a separate draft, not this RFC.

## Related Drafts & Updates

| Document | Relationship | Description |
|----------|-------------|-------------|
| [draft-ietf-idr-bgp-ls-sr-policy](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-idr-bgp-ls-sr-policy/) | Draft lineage | Draft that became RFC 9857 |
| [RFC 9830](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9830/) | Complement | Advertising Segment Routing Policies in BGP (SR Policy SAFI) |
| [RFC 9831](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9831/) | Complement | Segment Type Extensions for BGP SR Policy (incl. SRv6 segment types) |
| [RFC 9552](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9552/) | Base protocol | BGP-LS |

## Related

- [SR Policy](https://srv6.md/topics/sr-policy/) - Candidate paths, BSIDs, and controller-driven TE
- [Telemetry](https://srv6.md/topics/telemetry/) - Other ways to collect SRv6 state
- [RFC 9514](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9514/) - BGP-LS Extensions for SRv6
- [RFC 9603](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9603/) - PCEP Extensions for SRv6

# RFC 10038 Explained: Distributing SRv6 Locators via DHCPv6

URL: https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc10038/
Path: rfcs/rfc10038.md
Summary: RFC 10038 explained in plain language: Distributing the SRv6 Locator Using DHCPv6 — IA_SRV6_LOCATOR and IA Locator options. What it defines, how it works and how it fits into SRv6 networks.

# RFC 10038 - SRv6 Locator Distribution via DHCPv6

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Title** | Distributing the Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) Locator Using DHCPv6 |
| **Authors** | W. Cheng (Ed.), R. Han, C. Lin (Ed.), D. Voyer, G. Zhang |
| **Date** | August 2026 |
| **Status** | Proposed Standard |
| **Link** | [datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc10038](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc10038/) |

## Summary

Every SRv6 endpoint needs a locator, and today that is almost always configured by hand or pushed by a management system. RFC 10038 lets an SRv6 node obtain its locator from a **DHCPv6 server**, using the same lease model that DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation already uses for customer prefixes.

The motivating case comes from broadband networks (the authors include China Mobile and New H3C): operator-managed **CPEs** sit behind a BRAS that already runs or relays DHCPv6, and the operator wants CPE-to-CPE SRv6 tunnels. Instead of configuring a locator on each CPE, the CPE requests one; the BRAS (as server or relay) installs a route for the locator toward the CPE and advertises it into the IGP. When the lease is released or expires, the route is withdrawn.

The RFC only covers getting the locator. How the node then allocates SIDs from it, and how it advertises those SIDs, is out of scope.

## Key Sections

| Section | Topic | Description |
|---------|-------|-------------|
| 3 | Motivation | CPE → BRAS → backbone broadband topology with CPE-to-CPE SRv6 |
| 4.1 | IA_SRV6_LOCATOR Option | Identity Association container with IAID, T1, T2 |
| 4.2 | IA Locator Option | The locator itself, lifetimes, algorithm and SID structure lengths |
| 5 | Procedures | Solicit/Advertise/Request/Reply, Renew/Rebind/Release, client, server and relay behavior |
| 5.5 | Route Advertisement | Server or relay installs and advertises the locator route |
| 8 | Security | Client and server must be inside one trusted SR domain |

## New DHCPv6 Codepoints

| Code | Name | Type |
|------|------|------|
| 149 | `OPTION_IA_SRV6_LOCATOR` | Option (IA container) |
| 150 | `OPTION_IALOCATOR` | Option (carries one locator) |
| 23 | `NoSRv6LocatorAvail` | Status code |

## IA Locator Option Fields

| Field | Size | Meaning |
|-------|------|---------|
| Preferred / Valid lifetime | 4 + 4 octets | Same semantics as delegated prefixes; `0xffffffff` = infinity |
| Algorithm | 1 octet | IGP algorithm the locator belongs to (0 = default, 128-255 = [Flex-Algo](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9350/)) |
| LB-Len / LN-Len | 1 + 1 octet | Locator Block and Locator Node lengths in bits |
| Fun-Len / Arg-Len | 1 + 1 octet | Function and Argument lengths in bits |
| SRv6-Locator | 0-16 octets | The locator, encoded in the minimum octets for LB-Len + LN-Len |

The four lengths must add up to at most 128 bits, and LB-Len + LN-Len must be non-zero. A client may send lengths with `::` as the locator to hint at the size it wants, much like a prefix-length hint in IA_PD.

## Lease Flow

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as DHCPv6 Client (CPE)
    participant S as DHCPv6 Server / Relay (BRAS)
    participant R as Upstream Routers
    C->>S: Solicit (empty IA_SRV6_LOCATOR)
    S->>C: Advertise (IA Locator)
    C->>S: Request (IA Locator)
    S->>C: Reply (IA Locator + lengths)
    S->>R: Install and advertise locator route
    Note over C: Allocate SIDs from locator
    C->>S: Release (or lease expires)
    S->>R: Withdraw locator route
```

| Locator algorithm | How the server/relay advertises it |
|-------------------|-------------------------------------|
| 0 (default) | Ordinary IP prefix reachability |
| Non-zero (Flex-Algo) | Must use the SRv6 Locator TLV ([RFC 9352](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9352/) / [RFC 9513](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9513/)) |

Multiple locators (for example, one best-effort and one low-latency Flex-Algo locator) are requested with multiple IA_SRV6_LOCATOR options; the RFC recommends asking for one larger locator up front rather than adding more later.

!!! warning "Common Pitfalls"
    - The DHCPv6 client and server **must** be in the same trusted SR domain. A CPE on customer premises is acceptable only if the operator fully manages it, and it must filter SRv6 traffic on both internal and external interfaces per RFC 8754 Section 5.1.
    - DHCPv6 has no end-to-end encryption; a rogue client can impersonate many clients and drain the locator pool. Configure per-client limits.
    - If some nodes get locators from DHCPv6 and others are configured manually, draw them from non-overlapping pools to avoid duplicates.
    - Aggregating locator routes at the BRAS hides individual withdrawals; decide whether per-CPE routes or an aggregate is advertised.
    - The client must not infer service meaning from the order of returned locators.

## Related Drafts & Updates

| Document | Relationship | Description |
|----------|-------------|-------------|
| [draft-ietf-spring-dhc-distribute-srv6-locator-dhcp](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-spring-dhc-distribute-srv6-locator-dhcp/) | Draft lineage | Draft that became RFC 10038 |
| [RFC 9915](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9915/) | Base protocol | DHCPv6 specification whose IA_PD procedures this RFC reuses |
| [RFC 9800](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9800/) | Applies to | Locators from DHCPv6 may be used for NEXT/REPLACE C-SIDs |

## Related

- [Host-Based SRv6](https://srv6.md/topics/host-based-srv6/) - SRv6 on hosts and CPE-class Linux devices
- [SID Structure](https://srv6.md/topics/sid-structure/) - Locator Block / Node / Function / Argument layout
- [RFC 8986](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc8986/) - SRv6 Network Programming (locator definition)

## References

2. [RFC 9915](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9915/) - Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6)
3. [RFC 8986](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8986/) - SRv6 Network Programming (SID structure, Section 3.1)

# RFC 9252 Explained: BGP Overlay Services over SRv6

URL: https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9252/
Path: rfcs/rfc9252.md
Summary: RFC 9252 explained in plain language: BGP Overlay Services Based on SRv6. What it defines, how it works and how it fits into SRv6 networks.

# RFC 9252 - BGP Overlay Services Based on SRv6

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Title** | BGP Overlay Services Based on Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) |
| **Authors** | G. Dawra, et al. |
| **Date** | July 2022 |
| **Status** | Proposed Standard |
| **Link** | [datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9252](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9252/) |

## Summary

Defines how BGP carries SRv6 SID information for L3VPN (VPNv4/VPNv6) and L2VPN (EVPN) overlay services, using the SRv6 Services TLVs in BGP updates.

## Key Concepts

- **SRv6 L3 Service TLV** in BGP prefix-SID attribute
- **Transposition** of SID function into the IPv6 prefix
- Works with existing BGP VPN address families
- Enables MPLS-free VPN services

## Key Sections

| Section | Topic | Description |
|---------|-------|-------------|
| 3 | SRv6 Services TLVs | Defines the SRv6 L3 Service TLV and SRv6 L2 Service TLV carried in the BGP Prefix-SID attribute |
| 3.1 | SRv6 SID Information Sub-TLV | Carries the SRv6 SID value, SID behavior, and SID structure |
| 3.2 | SRv6 SID Structure Sub-Sub-TLV | Describes Locator Block, Locator Node, Function, and Argument bit lengths within the SID |
| 4 | Encoding for L3VPN | How VPNv4 and VPNv6 NLRI are encoded with SRv6 SIDs using the SRv6 L3 Service TLV |
| 4.1 | Transposition | Mechanism to embed the SRv6 Function value into the IPv6 prefix NLRI to save BGP update space |
| 5 | Encoding for EVPN | How EVPN routes carry SRv6 SIDs for L2VPN and L3VPN-over-EVPN services |
| 6 | Color Extended Community | Used in conjunction with SR Policy (RFC 9256) to steer VPN traffic into specific SRv6 TE paths |
| 7 | Security Considerations | Trust model for SRv6 VPN SID advertisements |

### SRv6 Service TLVs Detail

The BGP Prefix-SID attribute carries service-specific TLVs:

| TLV | Type Value | Used By | Content |
|-----|-----------|---------|---------|
| **SRv6 L3 Service TLV** | 5 | VPNv4, VPNv6 | Contains one or more SRv6 SID Information sub-TLVs for L3VPN |
| **SRv6 L2 Service TLV** | 6 | EVPN | Contains SRv6 SID Information sub-TLVs for L2VPN/EVPN |
| **SRv6 SID Information Sub-TLV** | 1 | Both | Carries: SRv6 SID (16 bytes), SID Flags, Endpoint Behavior |
| **SRv6 SID Structure Sub-Sub-TLV** | 1 | Both | Locator Block Length, Locator Node Length, Function Length, Argument Length, Transposition Length, Transposition Offset |

### Transposition Mechanism

Transposition is an optimization that avoids carrying the full 128-bit SID in the BGP update by embedding the Function portion into the advertised IPv6 prefix:

```
Without Transposition:
  NLRI = IPv6 VPN prefix
  SRv6 SID = Full 128-bit SID in TLV

With Transposition:
  NLRI = IPv6 VPN prefix with Function bits embedded
  SRv6 SID = SID with Function bits zeroed (receiver reconstructs)

Reconstruction: Take Transposition Length bits starting at
  Transposition Offset from the NLRI, insert them into the SID
```

The receiver extracts the transposed bits from the NLRI and inserts them into the SID at the specified offset to reconstruct the full SID.

!!! warning "Common Pitfalls"

    **Transposition bit handling.** The Transposition Length and Transposition Offset fields must be set consistently between the SRv6 SID Structure sub-sub-TLV and the NLRI encoding. If the Function Length, Transposition Length, and Transposition Offset do not align, the receiving PE will reconstruct an incorrect SID. This is one of the most common interoperability issues in multi-vendor SRv6 VPN deployments.

    **SID Structure signaling is mandatory.** The SRv6 SID Structure sub-sub-TLV must be present when transposition is used. Without it, the receiving PE cannot determine how to reconstruct the SID from the NLRI. Some early implementations omitted this, leading to black-holed VPN traffic.

    **Endpoint Behavior must match the VPN type.** The Endpoint Behavior field in the SID Information sub-TLV (e.g., End.DT4, End.DT6, End.DX2) must correspond to the actual programmed behavior on the egress PE. A mismatch causes the egress PE to reject the SID or misprocess the packet.

    **Color Extended Community is separate from the SRv6 SID.** The Color Extended Community is used to steer traffic into SR Policies (RFC 9256). It does not replace or modify the SRv6 VPN SID -- it works alongside it for traffic engineering.

## Related Drafts & Updates

| Document | Relationship | Description |
|----------|-------------|-------------|
| [RFC 9819](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9819/) | **Updates RFC 9252** | Specifies argument signaling for End.DT2M ESI filtering (replaces the bitwise-OR of Section 6.3); transposition rules unchanged |
| [RFC 9723](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9723/) | Builds on | Colored Prefix Routing: intent-aware inter-AS steering of RFC 9252 service SIDs |
| [RFC 9800](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9800/) | Extension | Compressed SID (C-SID) support changes how SID Structure is signaled |
| [RFC 8986](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc8986/) | Defines behaviors | End.DT4, End.DT6, End.DX4, etc. behaviors referenced by this RFC |
| [draft-ietf-bess-srv6-services-ext](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-bess-srv6-services-ext/) | Extension | Additional SRv6 service extensions for BGP |

## Related

- [VPN Services](https://srv6.md/use-cases/vpn-services/)
- [RFC 8986](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc8986/) - SRv6 behaviors used by VPNs

# RFC 9256 Explained: Segment Routing Policy Architecture

URL: https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9256/
Path: rfcs/rfc9256.md
Summary: RFC 9256 explained in plain language: Segment Routing Policy Architecture. What it defines, how it works and how it fits into SRv6 networks.

# RFC 9256 - SR Policy Architecture

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Title** | Segment Routing Policy Architecture |
| **Authors** | C. Filsfils, et al. |
| **Date** | July 2022 |
| **Status** | Proposed Standard |
| **Link** | [datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9256](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9256/) |

## Summary

Defines the architecture for SR Policies - the mechanism used to steer traffic through specific paths in an SR network. Applicable to both SR-MPLS and SRv6.

## Key Concepts

- **SR Policy** = (headend, color, endpoint)
- **Candidate Paths** - multiple paths with preferences
- **Segment Lists** - ordered list of SIDs per candidate path
- **Binding SID (BSID)** - single SID representing an SR Policy

## Key Sections

| Section | Topic | Description |
|---------|-------|-------------|
| 2 | SR Policy Model | Defines the SR Policy as the tuple **(headend, color, endpoint)** and the hierarchical structure of candidate paths and segment lists |
| 2.1 | Candidate Paths | Multiple paths per policy, each with a preference value; highest preference wins |
| 2.2 | Segment Lists (SID Lists) | Ordered list of SIDs representing a source-routed path; each candidate path may have multiple weighted segment lists for ECMP |
| 2.3 | Protocol-Origin | How candidate paths are instantiated: via configuration, BGP (RFC 9830 SR Policy SAFI), or PCEP |
| 2.4 | Discriminator | Unique identifier within a protocol-origin to distinguish multiple candidate paths from the same source |
| 3 | Binding SID (BSID) | A single SID that represents an entire SR Policy; traffic steered to the BSID follows the policy's active path |
| 3.1 | BSID and Policy Lifecycle | BSID may be explicitly allocated or dynamically assigned; it remains stable across candidate path changes |
| 4 | Validity of SR Policy | Conditions under which a policy is operationally valid (at least one valid candidate path with a valid segment list) |
| 5 | Weighted ECMP | When a candidate path has multiple segment lists, traffic is distributed across them based on assigned weights |
| 6 | Steering into SR Policy | Mechanisms for directing traffic: BSID-based, color-based (BGP Color Extended Community), or per-destination steering |
| 7 | Security Considerations | Authorization of policy sources, BSID protection |

### SR Policy Identification

An SR Policy is uniquely identified by the combination of:

| Component | Description | Example |
|-----------|-------------|---------|
| **Headend** | The node where the policy is instantiated | Router-A (2001:db8::1) |
| **Color** | A 32-bit numeric value representing an intent or SLA class | 100 (low-latency) |
| **Endpoint** | The destination/far-end of the policy | Router-Z (2001:db8::9) |

### Candidate Path Selection

When multiple candidate paths exist for a policy, the selection follows this order:

1. **Preference** -- Highest numeric preference wins
2. **Protocol-Origin** -- If preference ties: PCEP (30) > BGP (20) > Configuration (10)
3. **Discriminator** -- Final tiebreaker within the same protocol-origin

!!! warning "Common Pitfalls"

    **BSID allocation must be unique per headend.** Each Binding SID must uniquely identify a single SR Policy on a given headend. If two policies inadvertently share a BSID, traffic may be steered into the wrong policy. Some implementations dynamically allocate BSIDs to avoid conflicts, but explicit allocation requires careful planning.

    **Candidate path preference is NOT the same as route preference.** SR Policy candidate path preference is an internal ordering mechanism within a single policy. It does not interact with BGP Local Preference, IGP metric, or other routing protocol preferences. A higher candidate path preference means that path is preferred, but this only matters among candidate paths of the *same* SR Policy.

    **A policy with no valid candidate path is operationally down.** If all candidate paths have invalid segment lists (e.g., unresolvable SIDs), the entire SR Policy becomes invalid. Traffic previously steered via the policy's BSID will be dropped or fall back depending on the implementation.

    **Weighted ECMP requires careful weight assignment.** When a candidate path has multiple segment lists with weights, the traffic split is proportional to the weights (e.g., weights 1:3 means 25%/75%). Setting all weights to 1 produces equal distribution. A weight of 0 is not valid.

    **Color is not a priority.** The Color value (32-bit integer) is an opaque identifier for intent. A higher color value does not mean higher priority -- it simply identifies a different SLA class or steering intent. Color matching is exact.

## Related Drafts & Updates

| Document | Relationship | Description |
|----------|-------------|-------------|
| [RFC 9830](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9830/) | Protocol | BGP SR Policy SAFI for distributing SR Policies via BGP (formerly draft-ietf-idr-sr-policy-safi) |
| [RFC 9603](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9603/) | Protocol | PCEP extensions for SRv6 candidate paths |
| [RFC 9857](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9857/) | Protocol | BGP-LS reporting of SR Policy candidate-path state |
| [RFC 9960](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9960/) | Extension | SR P2MP Policy reuses the candidate-path model for multicast trees |
| [draft-ietf-idr-sr-policy-path-segment](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-idr-sr-policy-path-segment/) | Extension | Path Segment for SR Policy to enable path identification |
| [draft-ietf-pce-segment-routing-policy-cp](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-pce-segment-routing-policy-cp/) | Protocol | PCEP extensions for SR Policy candidate paths |
| [RFC 9252](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9252/) | Uses Color | BGP Overlay Services use the Color Extended Community for SR Policy steering |

## Related

- [Traffic Engineering](https://srv6.md/use-cases/traffic-engineering/)
- [RFC 8986](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc8986/) - SRv6 Network Programming

# RFC 9433 Explained: SRv6 Mobile User Plane (MUP)

URL: https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9433/
Path: rfcs/rfc9433.md
Summary: RFC 9433 explained in plain language: SRv6 SID for Mobile User Plane (MUP). What it defines, how it works and how it fits into SRv6 networks.

# RFC 9433 - Segment Routing over IPv6 for the Mobile User Plane

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Title** | Segment Routing over IPv6 for the Mobile User Plane |
| **Authors** | S. Matsushima, C. Filsfils, M. Kohno, P. Camarillo, D. Voyer, C. Perkins |
| **Date** | July 2023 |
| **Status** | Proposed Standard |
| **Link** | [datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9433](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9433/) |

## Summary

RFC 9433 defines how SRv6 can be used as the mobile user plane protocol in 3GPP networks, replacing GTP-U tunneling between mobile network functions. By encoding mobile session state directly into SRv6 SIDs, the architecture eliminates the need for GTP-U encapsulation between the UPF (User Plane Function) nodes, reducing per-packet overhead and simplifying the data plane.

The document specifies several new SRv6 endpoint behaviors purpose-built for mobile user plane interworking. These behaviors handle the translation between GTP-U and SRv6 at network boundaries and the pure SRv6 forwarding within the mobile transport. The SID structure carries mobile-specific arguments such as QFI (QoS Flow Identifier) and TEID (Tunnel Endpoint Identifier) information, enabling stateless translation at domain boundaries.

This approach allows operators to converge their mobile backhaul and transport networks onto a single SRv6 infrastructure, reducing operational complexity while enabling advanced capabilities like network slicing using SRv6 and Flex-Algo.

## Key Sections

| Section | Topic | Description |
|---------|-------|-------------|
| 3 | Reference Architecture | 5G user plane architecture with SRv6 replacing GTP-U |
| 4 | SRv6 SID for Mobile User Plane | SID structure carrying mobile session context |
| 5 | SRv6 Endpoint Behaviors | New behaviors for GTP-U interworking |
| 6 | Uplink and Downlink Scenarios | Packet flow for both directions |
| 7 | IPv4 User Plane Support | Handling IPv4 UE traffic over SRv6 |

## MUP Endpoint Behaviors

| Behavior | Direction | Function |
|----------|-----------|----------|
| **End.M.GTP6.D** | Downlink | Decapsulates SRv6 and encapsulates into GTP-U toward the gNB (IPv6 payload) |
| **End.M.GTP6.Di** | Downlink | Same as above but for IPv6 traffic with inner header insertion |
| **End.M.GTP6.E** | Uplink | Decapsulates GTP-U from gNB and encapsulates into SRv6 |
| **End.M.GTP4.E** | Uplink | Decapsulates GTP-U (IPv4 outer) and encapsulates into SRv6 |
| **H.M.GTP4.D** | Downlink | Headend behavior: encodes GTP-U parameters into SRv6 SID args for IPv4 N3 |

## MUP SID Structure

The MUP SID encodes mobile session information directly in the SRv6 SID:

```
|<-------- Locator -------->|<-- Function -->|<--- Argument --->|
|   Block     |    Node     |    Behavior    |  TEID + QFI etc  |
```

| Field | Purpose |
|-------|---------|
| **Locator** | Identifies the UPF or mobile anchor node |
| **Function** | Identifies the MUP behavior (e.g., End.M.GTP6.D) |
| **Argument** | Carries TEID, QFI, and other GTP-U session parameters |

## GTP-U to SRv6 Interworking

| Scenario | Source | Translation Point | Destination |
|----------|--------|-------------------|-------------|
| Uplink (N3) | gNB sends GTP-U | Ingress UPF: GTP-U to SRv6 | Anchor UPF (SRv6 endpoint) |
| Downlink (N3) | Anchor UPF sends SRv6 | Egress UPF: SRv6 to GTP-U | gNB receives GTP-U |
| N9 (inter-UPF) | UPF sends SRv6 | No translation needed | UPF receives SRv6 |

!!! warning "Common Pitfalls"
    - The MUP behaviors require the argument portion of the SID to be large enough to encode the TEID (32 bits) and QFI (6 bits). An undersized Locator:Function leaves insufficient room for arguments.
    - The interworking functions at domain boundaries must maintain awareness of the GTP-U tunnel state for proper TEID mapping, even though the SRv6 core is stateless.
    - IPv4 user plane traffic requires special handling (End.M.GTP4.E / H.M.GTP4.D) because of the different N3 encapsulation header format.
    - Deploying MUP without Flex-Algo for network slicing loses one of the key benefits -- the ability to map 5G network slices to distinct SRv6 topologies.
    - Not all SRv6 implementations support MUP behaviors. Verify platform support before planning a GTP-U replacement deployment.

## Related Drafts & Updates

- [draft-ietf-dmm-srv6-mobile-uplane](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-dmm-srv6-mobile-uplane/) - Earlier draft lineage of this work
- [draft-mhkk-dmm-srv6mup-architecture](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-mhkk-dmm-srv6mup-architecture/) - SRv6 MUP architecture extensions

## Related

- [RFC 8402](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc8402/) - Segment Routing Architecture
- [RFC 8986](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc8986/) - SRv6 Network Programming
- [RFC 8754](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc8754/) - IPv6 Segment Routing Header (SRH)
- [RFC 9350](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9350/) - IGP Flexible Algorithm (for network slicing)

## References

1. [RFC 9433](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9433/) - Segment Routing over IPv6 for the Mobile User Plane
2. [RFC 8986](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8986/) - SRv6 Network Programming
3. [3GPP TS 29.281](https://www.3gpp.org/DynaReport/29281.htm) - GPRS Tunnelling Protocol User Plane (GTPv1-U)
4. [3GPP TS 23.501](https://www.3gpp.org/DynaReport/23501.htm) - 5G System Architecture

# RFC 9723 Explained: BGP Colored Prefix Routing for SRv6

URL: https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9723/
Path: rfcs/rfc9723.md
Summary: RFC 9723 explained in plain language: BGP Colored Prefix Routing (CPR) for SRv6 services — intent-aware inter-domain paths via colored locators. What it defines, how it works and how it fits into SRv6 networks.

# RFC 9723 - BGP Colored Prefix Routing (CPR)

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Title** | BGP Colored Prefix Routing (CPR) for Services Based on Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) |
| **Authors** | H. Wang, J. Dong, K. Talaulikar, T. Han, R. Chen |
| **Date** | May 2025 |
| **Status** | Informational |
| **Link** | [datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9723](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9723/) |

## Summary

RFC 9723 describes how to deliver **intent-aware (color-aware) SRv6 services across multiple ASes without any new BGP extension**. The trick is to put the intent into the locator: each PE splits its base locator into **sub-locators, one per intent** (low delay, high bandwidth, ...). These *Colored Prefixes* are advertised in plain BGP **IPv6 unicast (AFI/SAFI 2/1)** with a **Color Extended Community**.

Service SIDs are then allocated from the colored sub-locator that matches the service's intent — e.g., a low-latency VPN gets its End.DT4 SID from the low-delay locator. Service routes are advertised as usual ([RFC 9252](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9252/), Option C, next hop unchanged) and need no color of their own. Ingress PEs and border routers simply do **longest-prefix match** of the service SID against the colored prefix, and resolve that route onto an intra-domain path for the tuple *(next hop, color)* — an SRv6 Policy, SRv6 Flex-Algo, or even an SR-MPLS/RSVP-TE LSP in MPLS transit domains.

Because the packet's destination is always the service SID, no inter-domain transport label or SID is needed, keeping encapsulation small.

## Key Sections

| Section | Topic | Description |
|---------|-------|-------------|
| 2.1 | Colored Prefix Allocation | Split the base locator into per-intent sub-locators |
| 2.2 | Advertisement | IPv6 unicast + Color Extended Community across ASes; color re-mapping at borders |
| 2.3 | Path Resolution | Resolve on (next hop, color) to SRv6/SR-MPLS Policy, Flex-Algo, or RSVP-TE |
| 2.4-2.5 | Service Routes and Steering | Service SIDs under colored locators; LPM steering |
| 3 | Encapsulation | Packet walks over SRv6 and MPLS intra-domain paths |
| 4 | Operational Considerations | Trust model, aggregation, fallback in legacy domains, 5f00::/16 filtering |

## Example Allocation

| Prefix | Intent | Advertised with |
|--------|--------|-----------------|
| `2001:db8:aaaa:1::/64` | Base locator | No color |
| `2001:db8:aaaa:1:0000::/68` | Color 1 (e.g., low delay) | Color Extended Community C1 |
| `2001:db8:aaaa:1:1000::/68` | Color 2 (e.g., high bandwidth) | Color Extended Community C2 |
| ... up to `2001:db8:aaaa:1:f000::/68` | 16 intents total | ... |

## CPR vs Other Intent-Aware Approaches

| Approach | Signaling | Intent carried in | Border-node data plane |
|----------|-----------|-------------------|------------------------|
| **CPR (RFC 9723)** | Existing IPv6 unicast SAFI + Color EC | Service SID's locator | Plain IPv6 forwarding (re-encapsulate per domain) |
| **BGP-CAR** | Separate SAFI | Locator prefix | Similar, with dedicated SAFI |
| **BGP-CT** | Classful Transport SAFI | Additional transport SID | SRv6 operation similar to label swap |
| **Inter-domain SR Policy** | Controller / BSID | Segment list | Policy stitching |

!!! warning "Common Pitfalls"
    - CPR assumes all participating ASes are one **trusted domain** (same operator or a formal trust model). Colored locators are ordinary IPv6 unicast routes, so boundary filters must keep them from leaking.
    - **Disable aggregation** for IPv6 unicast routes carrying a Color Extended Community; otherwise the base locator swallows the colored sub-locators.
    - If one intent uses different color values in different ASes, borders must rewrite the Color EC according to a consistent mapping policy. The same colored prefix appearing with two colors is a misconfiguration.
    - Domains that do not support CPR fall back to best-effort resolution — the service still works, but the intent is not honored in that AS.
    - With `5f00::/16` ([RFC 9602](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9602/)) blocked by default at boundaries, explicitly permit the colored prefixes in use within the trusted domain.

## Related Drafts & Updates

| Document | Relationship | Description |
|----------|-------------|-------------|
| [draft-ietf-idr-cpr](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-idr-cpr/) | Draft lineage | Draft that became RFC 9723 |
| [draft-ietf-idr-bgp-car](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-idr-bgp-car/) | Alternative | BGP Color-Aware Routing (separate SAFI) |
| [draft-ietf-idr-bgp-ct](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-idr-bgp-ct/) | Alternative | BGP Classful Transport planes |

## Related

- [Inter-Domain SRv6](https://srv6.md/topics/inter-domain/) - Multi-AS design patterns and boundary options
- [Flex-Algorithm](https://srv6.md/topics/flex-algorithm/) - One intra-domain way to realize a color
- [RFC 9252](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9252/) - BGP Overlay Services Based on SRv6
- [RFC 9256](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9256/) - SR Policy Architecture (color semantics)

## References

1. [RFC 9723](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9723) - BGP Colored Prefix Routing (CPR) for SRv6 Services
2. [RFC 9012](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9012/) - BGP Tunnel Encapsulation Attribute (Color Extended Community)
3. [RFC 9252](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9252/) - BGP Overlay Services Based on SRv6
4. [RFC 9602](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9602/) - SRv6 SIDs in the IPv6 Addressing Architecture

# RFC 9819 Explained: Argument Signaling for SRv6 BGP Services

URL: https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9819/
Path: rfcs/rfc9819.md
Summary: RFC 9819 explained in plain language: Argument Signaling for BGP Services in SRv6 — End.DT2M ESI filtering argument (updates RFC 9252). What it defines, how it works and how it fits into SRv6 networks.

# RFC 9819 - Argument Signaling for BGP Services in SRv6

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Title** | Argument Signaling for BGP Services in Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) |
| **Authors** | K. Talaulikar, K. Raza, J. Rabadan, W. Lin |
| **Date** | July 2025 |
| **Status** | Proposed Standard |
| **Updates** | [RFC 9252](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9252/) |
| **Link** | [datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9819](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9819/) |

## Summary

Some SRv6 behaviors take an **argument** in the low-order bits of the SID. The case that matters for BGP services is **End.DT2M** (EVPN BUM flooding), whose argument `Arg.FE2` tells the egress PE which local Ethernet Segment to exclude — the split-horizon (ESI filtering) needed for EVPN multihoming and E-Tree leaf filtering.

[RFC 9252](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9252/) split the signaling: the egress PE advertises the `LOC:FUNC` part of its End.DT2M SID in the **Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag route (Type 3)** and the argument in the **Ethernet A-D per ES route (Type 1)**, and the ingress PE combined them with a bitwise OR. Interop testing showed this was ambiguous and only works if both routes use identical SID structures. RFC 9819 replaces the OR with an explicit procedure: the ingress PE inserts the argument at the offset given by the SID Structure (LBL + LNL + FL) of the Type 3 route.

The rules are written for End.DT2M but apply to any argument-carrying SRv6 behavior signaled in BGP, and they cover the compressed (NEXT-C-SID) End.DT2M flavors from [RFC 9800](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9800/) as well.

## Key Sections

| Section | Topic | Description |
|---------|-------|-------------|
| 2 | Advertisement of SID and Arguments | SID Structure sub-sub-TLV is mandatory; AL = 0 means "no argument accepted" |
| 3.1 | Ethernet A-D per ES route | Carries the ESI filtering argument (or `::` with AL = 0) |
| 3.2 | Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag route | Carries only `LOC:FUNC`; AL announces the argument size |
| 3.3 | Ingress PE processing | How to build the data-plane SID and what to do on inconsistent AL |
| 4 | Backward compatibility | When the RFC 9252 bitwise-OR still works |

## Signaling Rules

| Route | SID field | Argument Length (AL) |
|-------|-----------|----------------------|
| Type 1 (A-D per ES), no ESI filtering | `::` (End.DT2M), structure still included | 0 |
| Type 1 (A-D per ES), ESI filtering | Argument value placed at LBL+LNL+FL offset | Argument size (SHOULD be a multiple of 8) |
| Type 3 (IMET), no ESI filtering | `LOC:FUNC` only | 0 |
| Type 3 (IMET), ESI filtering | `LOC:FUNC` only | Must equal the AL in the Type 1 route |

## Ingress PE Decision

| Condition | Result |
|-----------|--------|
| Type 3 AL = 0 | Use `LOC:FUNC` only; ignore any Type 1 argument |
| Type 3 AL ≠ 0, no matching Type 1 SID or Type 1 AL = 0 | No usable argument; use `LOC:FUNC` only |
| Both AL ≠ 0 but **different** | Configuration error — **do not forward BUM** from that ES to avoid loops; log it |
| Both AL ≠ 0 and equal | Insert the Type 1 argument at offset LBL+LNL+FL of the Type 3 SID |

Example from the RFC: Type 3 `2001:db8:1:fbd1::` (structure 32/16/16, AL 16) plus Type 1 argument `aaaa` gives the data-plane SID `2001:db8:1:fbd1:aaaa::`. With a 32-bit function on another bridge domain, the same argument lands one hextet further right — something a plain OR could not express.

!!! warning "Common Pitfalls"
    - Older RFC 9252-only implementations that OR the two SIDs interoperate only when both routes advertise **the same SID structure**. Mixed structures require RFC 9819 support on the ingress PE.
    - An egress PE must use the same AL for all local Ethernet Segments in a broadcast domain.
    - Do not "simplify" the Type 1 encoding by zeroing LBL/LNL/FL — it breaks backward compatibility with RFC 9252 receivers.
    - ESI filtering is not needed with the "Local Bias" method (RFC 8365), without multihoming, or without E-Tree leaf BUM traffic.

## Related Drafts & Updates

| Document | Relationship | Description |
|----------|-------------|-------------|
| [RFC 9252](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9252/) | Updated by this RFC | BGP overlay services over SRv6 |
| [draft-ietf-bess-bgp-srv6-args](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-bess-bgp-srv6-args/) | Draft lineage | Draft that became RFC 9819 |

## Related

- [EVPN Multihoming](https://srv6.md/topics/evpn-multihoming/) - Split horizon and ESI filtering in practice
- [BGP Overlay Services](https://srv6.md/topics/bgp-overlay-services/) - EVPN and L3VPN over SRv6
- [RFC 8986](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc8986/) - End.DT2M and Arg.FE2 definitions
- [RFC 9800](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9800/) - Compressed End.DT2M flavors

## References

1. [RFC 9819](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9819) - Argument Signaling for BGP Services in SRv6
2. [RFC 9252](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9252/) - BGP Overlay Services Based on SRv6
3. [RFC 7432](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc7432/) - BGP MPLS-Based Ethernet VPN (route types, split horizon)
4. [RFC 8317](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8317/) - Ethernet-Tree (E-Tree) Support in EVPN

# RFC 9524 Explained: SR Replication Segment for Multicast

URL: https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9524/
Path: rfcs/rfc9524.md
Summary: RFC 9524 explained in plain language: Segment Routing Replication for Multipoint Service Delivery (Replication segment and End.Replicate). What it defines, how it works and how it fits into SRv6 networks.

# RFC 9524 - SR Replication Segment

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Title** | Segment Routing Replication for Multipoint Service Delivery |
| **Authors** | D. Voyer (Ed.), C. Filsfils, R. Parekh, H. Bidgoli, Z. Zhang |
| **Date** | February 2024 |
| **Status** | Proposed Standard |
| **Updated by** | [RFC 9960](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9960/) (Replication-ID structure) |
| **Link** | [datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9524](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9524/) |

## Summary

RFC 9524 adds a new segment type to the SR architecture: the **Replication segment**. A node that holds a Replication segment (the *replication node*) copies each packet it receives on that segment and sends one copy to each of a set of *downstream nodes*. The same construct works for SR-MPLS (a label) and SRv6 (a SID with the new **End.Replicate** behavior).

Unlike every other SRv6 behavior, End.Replicate is driven by **local replication state** rather than by the segment list. The replication node looks up the SID's FUNCT bits, finds its list of replication branches, and for each branch writes the downstream node's Replication-SID into the outer IPv6 destination address. Downstream nodes do not need to be adjacent: the locator of the downstream Replication-SID is enough to reach it over shortest path (default or Flex-Algo), or the replication node can add an `H.Encaps.Red` segment list to steer the copy over a TE path.

A single Replication segment whose downstream nodes are all the egress PEs is simply **ingress replication**. Stitching several Replication segments together (root → intermediate replication nodes → leaves) builds a **P2MP tree**; RFC 9524 deliberately leaves that stitching to a control plane, which [RFC 9960](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9960/) (SR P2MP Policy) defines.

## Key Sections

| Section | Topic | Description |
|---------|-------|-------------|
| 1.2 | Use Cases | Ingress replication for MVPN and EVPN BUM; trees built from stitched segments |
| 2 | Replication Segment | Identifier ``, Replication-SID, downstream nodes, replication state |
| 2.1 | SR-MPLS Data Plane | POP + per-branch PUSH of downstream Replication-SID |
| 2.2 | SRv6 Data Plane | DA rewrite, optional `H.Encaps.Red` per branch, Hop Limit handling |
| 2.2.1 | End.Replicate | Pseudocode for the replicate and/or decapsulate behavior |
| 2.2.2 | OAM | Pinging a leaf Replication-SID through transit replication nodes |
| 2.2.3 | ICMPv6 Errors | Same ICMPv6 restrictions as IPv6 multicast destinations |
| App. A | Illustration | Worked SR-MPLS and SRv6 examples |

## Node Roles and Terminology

| Term | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| **Replication node** | Node that replicates packets based on a Replication segment |
| **Downstream nodes** | The set of nodes a Replication segment sends copies to |
| **Replication state (RS)** | List of branches, each a `` pair (optionally with a segment list) |
| **Root** | Ingress node of the P2MP service (also a replication node) |
| **Leaf** | Egress node; its Replication segment has a leaf indicator and an empty branch list |
| **Bud** | Node that is both a replication node and a leaf |

## End.Replicate Processing (SRv6)

| Step | Action |
|------|--------|
| 1 | Look up the FUNCT part of the DA to find the replication state; drop if none |
| 2 | Drop if Hop Limit ≤ 1, or below the optional per-segment **Hop Limit Threshold** (rate-limited log) |
| 3 | Decrement Hop Limit; optionally process SRH TLVs |
| 4 | For each branch: copy the packet, set DA = downstream Replication-SID, optionally apply `H.Encaps`/`H.Encaps.Red` with the branch's segment list, then forward via the IPv6 FIB |
| 5 | If the node is a Leaf or Bud: derive the packet-processing context (from the next SID in the SRH or from the Replication-SID itself), strip the outer header, and process the inner IPv4/IPv6/Ethernet payload |

The SRH segment list is **not** advanced by a replication node — copies leave with the SRH unchanged. Any SIDs after the Replication-SID are context for leaf/bud nodes (for example, a service SID identifying the VPN).

| Codepoint | Value | Registry |
|-----------|-------|----------|
| End.Replicate | 75 (`0x004B`) | SRv6 Endpoint Behaviors |

## Ingress Replication vs Tree

| Model | Replication segments | Transit state |
|-------|---------------------|---------------|
| **Ingress replication** | One at the root; all leaves are downstream nodes | None beyond normal unicast forwarding |
| **P2MP tree** ([RFC 9960](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9960/)) | Root + intermediate replication nodes + leaves | Replication state on each replication node; plain transit routers forward on the locator |

!!! warning "Common Pitfalls"
    - End.Replicate is **stateful** at replication nodes. It is not "replication encoded in the SRH" — the branch list lives on the node and is programmed locally or by a controller.
    - ICMPv6 errors (Time Exceeded, Parameter Problem) must **not** be generated for Replication-SIDs, so traceroute to a leaf Replication-SID does not work. Use ping to a leaf/bud Replication-SID instead (Section 2.2.2).
    - Set the root's Hop Limit high enough to reach the furthest leaf; copying the payload's Hop Limit may strand distant leaves. Non-replicating routers on the path can otherwise expire packets and storm the root with ICMPv6.
    - When a branch uses `H.Encaps.Red` to reach a non-adjacent downstream node, the extra IPv6 header must fit the path MTU.
    - If an HMAC TLV is used with a context SID in the SRH, the root must set the SRH `D` bit because the Replication-SID is not in the segment list.
    - Locally provisioned chains of Replication segments must not form loops; RFC 9524 itself has no loop detection.

## Related Drafts & Updates

|----------|-------------|-------------|
| [RFC 9960](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9960/) | **Updates RFC 9524** | SR P2MP Policy; redefines the Replication-ID as `` |
| [draft-ietf-pce-sr-p2mp-policy](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-pce-sr-p2mp-policy/) | Control plane | PCEP extensions for instantiating Replication segments of P2MP trees |
| [draft-ietf-idr-sr-p2mp-policy](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-idr-sr-p2mp-policy/) | Control plane | Advertising P2MP policies in BGP |
| [draft-ietf-spring-sr-replication-segment](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-spring-sr-replication-segment/) | Draft lineage | Draft that became RFC 9524 |

- [Multicast & Broadcast](https://srv6.md/topics/multicast/) - Where replication segments fit among SRv6 multicast options

# RFC 9860 Explained: MoFRR Based on TI-LFA

URL: https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9860/
Path: rfcs/rfc9860.md
Summary: RFC 9860 explained in plain language: Multicast-only Fast Reroute (MoFRR) based on TI-LFA — PIM secondary joins along TI-LFA repair paths. What it defines, how it works and how it fits into SRv6 networks.

# RFC 9860 - MoFRR Based on TI-LFA

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Title** | Multicast-Only Fast Reroute (MoFRR) Based on Topology Independent Loop-Free Alternate (TI-LFA) Fast Reroute |
| **Authors** | Y. Liu, M. McBride, Z. Zhang, J. Xie, C. Lin |
| **Date** | October 2025 |
| **Status** | Informational |
| **Link** | [datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9860](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9860/) |

## Summary

**MoFRR** (RFC 7431) protects PIM multicast by joining the same (S,G) on two upstream paths and switching to the standby stream on failure. Its weakness is how it picks the secondary upstream hop: it relies on classic **LFA**, so in many topologies no loop-free secondary exists and MoFRR simply cannot protect the flow.

RFC 9860 borrows the repair path that [TI-LFA](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9855/) already computes for unicast — which has full topology coverage — and uses it to build the **standby multicast tree**. The catch is that PIM joins must be processed hop by hop to create state on every router, so they cannot just be tunneled along the repair segment list. Instead, the receiver-side router translates the repair segments into existing **PIM RPF Vector** attributes:

- a **Node SID / End SID** (the P-node or PQ-node) becomes an **RPF Vector** (RFC 5496) carrying that node's address;
- an **Adjacency SID / End.X SID** (P-node → Q-node link) becomes an **Explicit RPF Vector** (RFC 7891) carrying the far-end interface address.

The secondary join follows these vectors hop by hop, creating PIM state along the TI-LFA path. It works for both SR-MPLS and SRv6 IGP SIDs, and needs **no new protocol extensions** — only that every router on the backup join path supports RPF Vectors.

## Key Sections

| Section | Topic | Description |
|---------|-------|-------------|
| 2.1 | LFA for MoFRR | Why LFA-based secondary UMH fails in common topologies |
| 2.2 | TI-LFA for MoFRR | Why a segment list cannot be used directly for PIM joins |
| 3 | Solution | Mapping Node/Adjacency SIDs to RPF Vector and Explicit RPF Vector |
| 4 | Illustration | Worked SR-MPLS and SRv6 example |
| 5 | Operations | RPF Vector support requirements and debugging with mtrace |

## SID-to-PIM Mapping

| TI-LFA repair element | PIM Join attribute | Effect |
|-----------------------|--------------------|--------|
| Node SID / SRv6 End SID of P (or PQ) node | RPF Vector (Type 0) with node address | Join is routed toward the P-node instead of the source |
| Adj-SID / SRv6 End.X SID from P to Q | Explicit RPF Vector (Type 4) with remote interface address | P-node sends the join across that specific link |
| (after last vector) | No vector | Normal RPF toward the source from the Q-node |

When a single PQ-node exists, only one RPF Vector is needed.

!!! warning "Common Pitfalls"
    - Every router on the backup join path must understand RPF Vectors. A router that does not must strip them — leaving them in can loop the join back.
    - Scope is a single IGP area; exit routers and inter-domain links are not protected.
    - Micro-loops during reconvergence are not addressed for PIM.
    - This protects **PIM** trees. It does not apply to SRv6-native replication (RFC 9524 / RFC 9960) or BIER.
    - It is Informational and optional: deployments must explicitly configure when secondary joins with vectors are sent.

## Related Drafts & Updates

| Document | Relationship | Description |
|----------|-------------|-------------|
| [draft-ietf-pim-mofrr-tilfa](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-pim-mofrr-tilfa/) | Draft lineage | Draft that became RFC 9860 |
| [RFC 7431](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc7431/) | Base mechanism | Multicast-Only Fast Reroute |

## Related

- [TI-LFA](https://srv6.md/topics/ti-lfa/) - How the repair path is computed
- [Multicast & Broadcast](https://srv6.md/topics/multicast/) - Multicast options in SRv6 networks
- [RFC 9855](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9855/) - TI-LFA Using Segment Routing

## References

1. [RFC 9860](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9860) - MoFRR Based on TI-LFA Fast Reroute
2. [RFC 7431](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc7431/) - Multicast-Only Fast Reroute
3. [RFC 5496](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc5496/) - The RPF Vector TLV
4. [RFC 7891](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc7891/) - Explicit Reverse Path Forwarding (RPF) Vector

# RFC 9960 Explained: Segment Routing P2MP Policy (Tree-SID)

URL: https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9960/
Path: rfcs/rfc9960.md
Summary: RFC 9960 explained in plain language: Segment Routing Point-to-Multipoint (P2MP) Policy — Tree-SID architecture built from Replication segments. What it defines, how it works and how it fits into SRv6 networks.

# RFC 9960 - SR P2MP Policy

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Title** | Segment Routing Point-to-Multipoint Policy |
| **Authors** | R. Parekh (Ed.), D. Voyer (Ed.), C. Filsfils, H. Bidgoli, Z. Zhang |
| **Date** | April 2026 |
| **Status** | Proposed Standard |
| **Updates** | [RFC 9524](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9524/) |
| **Link** | [datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9960](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9960/) |

## Summary

RFC 9960 is the architecture behind **Tree-SID**. It defines the **SR P2MP Policy**: a construct, identified by ``, that names a root node and a set of leaf nodes and carries one or more candidate paths (CPs) with constraints and optimization objectives, reusing the candidate-path model and selection rules of [RFC 9256](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9256/).

A controller (typically a PCE) computes a **P2MP tree instance (PTI)** for each candidate path and instantiates it by programming [RFC 9524](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9524/) Replication segments on the root, the intermediate replication nodes, and the leaves. The Replication-SID at the root is the **Tree-SID**; the RFC recommends reusing the same value at every node of the instance to simplify troubleshooting. For SRv6, the Replication-SID is the FUNCT part of the SID, so even with a common Tree-SID value the locator differs per node.

It works for both SR-MPLS and SRv6, and it updates RFC 9524 by giving the Replication-ID a precise structure: ``.

## Key Sections

| Section | Topic | Description |
|---------|-------|-------------|
| 2 | SR P2MP Policy | Identification, components, candidate paths and tree instances |
| 3 | Steering | Local-policy steering at the root vs BSID/Tree-SID steering from upstream |
| 4 | P2MP Tree Instance | Leaf Replication segments, shared Replication segments, forwarding |
| 5 | Controller | Tree compute, SID management, instantiation order, protection |
| App. A | Illustration | SR-MPLS and SRv6 examples with adjacent and non-adjacent replication |

## Identifiers

| Identifier | Size / Scope | Purpose |
|------------|--------------|---------|
| **Tree-ID** | 32-bit, unique per root | Identifies the SR P2MP Policy together with the root address |
| **Instance-ID** | 16-bit, unique per policy | Identifies one PTI (e.g., old and new instance during make-before-break) |
| **Replication-ID** | `` | Updated RFC 9524 identifier; full control-plane key adds Node-ID |
| **Tree-SID** | Replication-SID at the root | Data-plane identifier of the PTI |
| **BSID** | Per policy | Steers traffic into the policy when the root is not the domain ingress |

Shared Replication segments (for example, one protecting the X→Y adjacency for many trees) use Root = `::`/`0.0.0.0` and Instance-ID = 0. The simple 32-bit Replication-ID of RFC 9524 maps to ``.

## How a Tree Is Built

```mermaid
graph TD
    PCE[Controller / PCE] -.->|Replication segment| R[Root]
    PCE -.->|Replication segment| M[Replication node]
    PCE -.->|Replication segment| L1[Leaf 1]
    PCE -.->|Replication segment| L2[Leaf 2]
    PCE -.->|Replication segment| L3[Leaf 3]
    R -->|copy, DA = M Replication-SID| M
    R -->|copy, DA = L1 Replication-SID| L1
    M -->|copy| L2
    M -->|copy| L3
```

| Step | Controller action |
|------|-------------------|
| 1 | Learn topology and node P2MP capability |
| 2 | Compute a loop-free tree for the active CP (constraints from RFC 9256 SR Policy) |
| 3 | Assign Replication-SIDs (from SRLB for SR-MPLS, or reserved blocks) and the BSID |
| 4 | Program leaves and intermediate nodes first, then the root, then activate the instance |
| 5 | On topology change, recompute — optionally via make-before-break with a new Instance-ID |

## SRv6-Specific Rules

| Rule | Why |
|------|-----|
| Leaf nodes **must** have a Replication segment | No penultimate-hop popping: the Tree-SID is in the IPv6 DA |
| Multiple services on one PTI need a service-context SID as the **last SID in the SRH** | Leaves derive the VPN/EVPN context from it |
| Non-adjacent downstream nodes are reached via the Replication-SID's locator, or an optional segment list | Same mechanics as RFC 9524 Section 2.2 |

## Protection

| Type | Mechanism |
|------|-----------|
| **Local** | Backup SR Policies per replication branch, or node-local LFA / [TI-LFA](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9855/) plus micro-loop avoidance |
| **Path** | A backup CP whose PTIs are disjoint from the active CP's PTIs |

!!! warning "Common Pitfalls"
    - RFC 9960 defines the architecture, not the signaling. PCEP ([draft-ietf-pce-sr-p2mp-policy](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-pce-sr-p2mp-policy/)) and BGP ([draft-ietf-idr-sr-p2mp-policy](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-idr-sr-p2mp-policy/)) encodings are still Internet-Drafts, so vendor implementations may differ.
    - Only one PTI of a CP may be active at a time; two active instances deliver duplicate traffic to leaves.
    - Allocating Replication-SIDs from the SRGB is not recommended — trees are local state and can exhaust the global block.
    - A statically provisioned tree does not adapt to topology changes.
    - If the root's Replication segment fails to install, the controller should tear the instance down rather than leave a partial tree.

## Related Drafts & Updates

| Document | Relationship | Description |
|----------|-------------|-------------|
| [RFC 9524](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9524/) | Updated by this RFC | Replication segment and End.Replicate |
| [draft-ietf-pce-sr-p2mp-policy](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-pce-sr-p2mp-policy/) | Signaling | PCEP extensions for SR P2MP Policy |
| [draft-ietf-idr-sr-p2mp-policy](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-idr-sr-p2mp-policy/) | Signaling | Advertising P2MP policies in BGP |
| [draft-ietf-pim-sr-p2mp-policy](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-pim-sr-p2mp-policy/) | Draft lineage | Draft that became RFC 9960 |

## Related

- [Multicast & Broadcast](https://srv6.md/topics/multicast/) - Tree-SID configuration and comparison with ingress replication and BIER
- [RFC 9524](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9524/) - SR Replication Segment

4. [draft-ietf-pce-sr-p2mp-policy](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-pce-sr-p2mp-policy/) - PCEP extensions for SR P2MP Policy (Internet-Draft)
