# RFC 9259 Explained: SRv6 OAM, Ping and Traceroute

URL: https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9259/
Path: rfcs/rfc9259.md
Summary: RFC 9259 explained in plain language: Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) in SRv6. What it defines, how it works and how it fits into SRv6 networks.

# RFC 9259 - Operations and Management of SRv6

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Title** | Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) in Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) |
| **Authors** | Z. Ali, C. Filsfils, S. Matsushima, D. Voyer, M. Chen |
| **Date** | June 2022 |
| **Status** | Proposed Standard |
| **Link** | [datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9259](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9259/) |

## Summary

RFC 9259 defines the OAM mechanisms for SRv6 networks. It specifies how existing OAM tools (ping, traceroute) work in an SRv6 environment and defines new SRv6-specific OAM behaviors.

## Key Concepts

### SRv6 OAM Behaviors

| Behavior | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| `End.OP` | OAM endpoint - punt packet to control plane for OAM processing |
| `End.OTP` | OAM endpoint with timestamp - adds timestamp before punting |

### Ping in SRv6

SRv6 ping uses ICMPv6 Echo Request/Reply with the SRH to verify reachability along an SRv6 path. The ping follows the segment list, allowing operators to verify end-to-end SRv6 connectivity.

### Traceroute in SRv6

SRv6 traceroute works by incrementing the IPv6 Hop Limit to discover each hop along the SRv6 path. Each intermediate node returns an ICMPv6 Time Exceeded message, revealing the path taken.

### Key Differences from Traditional OAM

- OAM packets carry the SRH to follow the same path as data traffic
- Intermediate nodes may or may not be SRv6-aware
- SRv6 OAM can validate both the underlay path and the overlay service

## Key Sections

| Section | Topic | Description |
|---------|-------|-------------|
| 3 | OAM Flag in SRH | Defines the O-flag (bit 0) in the SRH Flags field; when set, it indicates the packet is an OAM packet that should be processed by the OAM mechanism at each SRv6-capable node |
| 4 | SRv6 OAM Endpoint Behaviors | Specifies End.OP (OAM punt) and End.OTP (OAM with Timestamp) endpoint behaviors for OAM processing |
| 5 | SRv6 Ping | ICMPv6 Echo Request/Reply procedures for SRv6; the source constructs the ping packet with an SRH containing the target segment list |
| 5.1 | Ping to a SID | Ping a specific SRv6 SID by placing it as the final segment; verifies SID reachability |
| 5.2 | Ping to a Policy | Ping using the full segment list of an SR Policy; verifies end-to-end path connectivity |
| 6 | SRv6 Traceroute | Hop-by-hop discovery using incrementing IPv6 Hop Limit with SRH; each hop returns ICMPv6 Time Exceeded |
| 6.1 | Traceroute to a SID | Discovers the path to a specific SRv6 SID |
| 6.2 | Traceroute to a Policy | Discovers all hops along an SR Policy path |
| 7 | Security Considerations | Rate limiting, trust boundaries, and filtering of OAM packets |

### OAM Flag Detail

The **O-flag** (Bit 0 in the SRH Flags field) marks a packet as an OAM packet:

```
SRH Flags:
 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7
+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+
|O|    Unused   |
+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+
```

When the O-flag is set, an SR endpoint node may choose to process the packet as OAM (e.g., punt to control plane) rather than forwarding it in the data plane.

!!! warning "Common Pitfalls"

    **Rate limiting ICMPv6 is critical.** SRv6 OAM relies on ICMPv6 Echo and Time Exceeded messages. Without proper rate limiting, OAM traffic can be used for denial-of-service attacks or can overwhelm the control plane of transit and endpoint nodes. Implementations must apply ICMPv6 rate limiting consistent with RFC 4443.

    **Transit nodes may not respond to traceroute.** In SRv6, transit nodes (non-segment-endpoint routers between SRv6 nodes) forward packets based only on the IPv6 DA. They do not process the SRH and may not generate ICMPv6 Time Exceeded messages that include the SRH. This means traceroute output may show transit hops but without SRv6-specific context. Some transit nodes may even suppress ICMPv6 responses entirely.

    **O-flag processing is optional.** Not all SRv6 implementations process the O-flag. An endpoint that does not support OAM behaviors (End.OP / End.OTP) will process the packet as a regular data packet despite the flag being set. Operators must verify OAM support on all relevant nodes.

    **Ping to a SID verifies the control plane, not necessarily the data plane.** A successful SRv6 ping confirms that the SID is reachable and the node responds, but it does not guarantee that data traffic following the same segment list will be forwarded correctly (e.g., VRF binding, L2 cross-connect).

## Use Cases

- **Path verification** - Confirm traffic follows the intended SRv6 policy
- **Fault isolation** - Identify which segment in the path is failing
- **Performance monitoring** - Measure latency and loss per segment
- **SLA validation** - Verify service-level agreements on SRv6 paths

## Related Drafts & Updates

| Document | Relationship | Description |
|----------|-------------|-------------|
| [draft-ietf-ippm-ioam-srv6-options](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-ippm-ioam-srv6-options/) | Extension | In-situ OAM (IOAM) data fields carried in SRv6 extension headers for per-hop telemetry |
| [draft-filsfils-spring-path-tracing](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-filsfils-spring-path-tracing/) | Extension | Lightweight path tracing for SRv6 using a compressed per-hop record in the SRH TLV space |
| [RFC 8754](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc8754/) | Dependency | Defines the SRH Flags field where the OAM O-flag resides |
| [RFC 8986](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc8986/) | Defines behaviors | End.OP and End.OTP behaviors are registered in the SRv6 Endpoint Behaviors registry |

## Related

- [What is SRv6?](https://srv6.md/topics/what-is-srv6/) - SRv6 overview
- [RFC 8754](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc8754/) - SRH format
- [RFC 9352](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9352/) - IS-IS extensions for SRv6

# RFC 9487 Explained: Exporting SRv6 Information in IPFIX

URL: https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9487/
Path: rfcs/rfc9487.md
Summary: RFC 9487 explained in plain language: Export of SRv6 Information in IPFIX. What it defines, how it works and how it fits into SRv6 networks.

# RFC 9487 - Export of Segment Routing over IPv6 Information in IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX)

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Title** | Export of Segment Routing over IPv6 Information in IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) |
| **Authors** | T. Graf, B. Claise, P. Francois |
| **Date** | November 2023 |
| **Status** | Informational |
| **Link** | [datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9487](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9487/) |

## Summary

RFC 9487 defines new IPFIX (IP Flow Information Export) Information Elements for exporting SRv6-related data from network nodes to collectors. As SRv6 deployments grow, operators need visibility into how SRv6 traffic is forwarded -- which SIDs are being used, what segment lists packets carry, and how traffic maps to SR Policies. This RFC provides the telemetry building blocks to answer those questions.

The document specifies 11 new IPFIX Information Elements that capture the essential SRv6 forwarding state observed at a metering point. These elements cover the active SID in the IPv6 destination address, the full segment list from the SRH, the Segments Left value, Section Tag, and flags. Together, they enable a collector to reconstruct the SRv6 forwarding path a packet is following.

These IPFIX elements are essential for SRv6 network operations, enabling use cases such as traffic engineering validation (confirming packets follow the intended SR Policy), SLA monitoring (measuring per-path latency and loss), capacity planning (understanding per-SID traffic volumes), and troubleshooting (identifying packets with unexpected segment lists).

## Key Sections

| Section | Topic | Description |
|---------|-------|-------------|
| 3 | Use Cases | Traffic engineering verification, SLA monitoring, troubleshooting |
| 4 | New IPFIX Information Elements | Definition of 11 SRv6-specific IEs |
| 5 | Encoding | How SRv6 SIDs and segment lists are encoded in IPFIX records |
| 6 | Export Scenarios | Where in the network SRv6 IPFIX export is most useful |

## New IPFIX Information Elements

| IE Name | IE ID | Type | Description |
|---------|-------|------|-------------|
| **srhFlags** | 502 | unsigned8 | Flags field from the SRH |
| **srhTag** | 503 | unsigned16 | Tag field from the SRH |
| **srhSegmentIPv6** | 504 | ipv6Address | An individual SRv6 SID from the segment list |
| **srhActiveSegmentIPv6** | 505 | ipv6Address | The currently active SID (from IPv6 DA) |
| **srhSegmentIPv6BasicList** | 506 | basicList | Ordered list of all SRv6 SIDs in the SRH |
| **srhSegmentsIPv6Left** | 507 | unsigned8 | Segments Left value from the SRH |
| **srhIPv6Section** | 508 | unsigned8 | Section of the SRH being reported |
| **srhIPv6ActiveSegmentType** | 509 | unsigned8 | Type of the active segment (e.g., transit, endpoint) |
| **srhSegmentIPv6ListSection** | 510 | basicList | Section of the segment list for large SRHs |
| **srhSegmentsIPv6SectionLeft** | 511 | unsigned8 | Segments Left relative to the reported section |
| **srhIPv6SRHLength** | 512 | unsigned16 | Total length of the SRH in bytes |

## Export Use Cases

| Use Case | Key IEs Used | Benefit |
|----------|-------------|---------|
| **TE Verification** | srhSegmentIPv6BasicList, srhActiveSegmentIPv6 | Confirm packets follow the programmed SR Policy path |
| **SLA Monitoring** | srhActiveSegmentIPv6 + timestamps | Measure per-path latency and jitter |
| **Capacity Planning** | srhSegmentIPv6 + byte/packet counters | Understand traffic volumes per SID and segment list |
| **Troubleshooting** | srhFlags, srhSegmentsIPv6Left, full segment list | Identify unexpected forwarding behavior or misrouted packets |
| **Accounting** | srhActiveSegmentIPv6 + flow counters | Per-service or per-tenant traffic accounting |

## IPFIX Export Points in an SRv6 Network

| Export Point | What is Visible | Typical Use |
|-------------|----------------|-------------|
| **Headend (ingress)** | Full SRH with complete segment list | Verify SR Policy is applied correctly |
| **Transit node** | IPv6 DA (active SID); SRH if configured to inspect | Monitor per-SID traffic load |
| **Endpoint (egress)** | Final SID processing, decapsulated inner packet | End-to-end path validation |

!!! warning "Common Pitfalls"
    - Not all hardware supports deep SRH inspection for IPFIX export. Transit routers often only see the IPv6 destination address (active SID) and cannot export the full segment list without SRH parsing support.
    - The srhSegmentIPv6BasicList IE uses the IPFIX basicList structured data type (RFC 6313). Collectors must support structured data to parse this field correctly.
    - Large segment lists may exceed IPFIX template or record size limits. The srhSegmentIPv6ListSection and srhIPv6Section IEs provide a mechanism for sectioned export, but collector support varies.
    - SRv6 compressed SIDs (uSID, RFC 9800) appear as standard 128-bit IPv6 addresses in IPFIX. The collector needs additional context (the GIB prefix and C-SID length) to decompose containers into individual micro-SIDs.
    - IPFIX sampling configuration significantly affects telemetry accuracy for SRv6. Low sampling rates may miss short-lived or low-volume SRv6 flows entirely.

## Related Drafts & Updates

- [draft-ietf-opsawg-ipfix-srv6-srh](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-opsawg-ipfix-srv6-srh/) - Earlier draft lineage
- [draft-ietf-opsawg-ipfix-on-path-telemetry](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-opsawg-ipfix-on-path-telemetry/) - IPFIX for on-path telemetry

## Related

- [RFC 8754](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc8754/) - IPv6 Segment Routing Header (SRH)
- [RFC 8986](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc8986/) - SRv6 Network Programming
- [RFC 9259](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9259/) - Operations, Administration, and Maintenance in SRv6

## References

1. [RFC 9487](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9487/) - Export of Segment Routing over IPv6 Information in IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX)
2. [RFC 7011](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc7011/) - Specification of the IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Protocol
3. [RFC 6313](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc6313/) - Export of Structured Data in IPFIX
4. [RFC 8754](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8754/) - IPv6 Segment Routing Header (SRH)

# RFC 9855 Explained: TI-LFA Fast Reroute

URL: https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9855/
Path: rfcs/rfc9855.md
Summary: RFC 9855 explained in plain language: Topology Independent Fast Reroute Using Segment Routing (TI-LFA). What it defines, how it works and how it fits into SRv6 networks.

# RFC 9855 - TI-LFA

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Title** | Topology Independent Fast Reroute Using Segment Routing |
| **Authors** | A. Bashandy, S. Litkowski, C. Filsfils, P. Francois, B. Decraene, D. Voyer |
| **Date** | October 2025 |
| **Status** | Proposed Standard |
| **Working group** | RTGWG (draft-ietf-rtgwg-segment-routing-ti-lfa) |
| **Link** | [datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9855](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9855/) |

## Summary

RFC 9855 defines Topology Independent Loop-Free Alternate (TI-LFA), the fast-reroute mechanism for node and adjacency segments in Segment Routing networks. It builds on LFA ([RFC 5286](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5286)), Remote LFA ([RFC 7490](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7490)) and Directed LFA, and extends them to provide guaranteed coverage in any two-connected network running a link-state IGP — hence "topology independent". It protects against the failure of a single link, a single node or a single SRLG.

The defining choice is to repair onto the **expected post-convergence path**: the path the PLR will use once the IGP has converged without the failed resource. Because the repair path matches the final path, traffic does not move twice, and operators do not need to tune tie-breaks between many possible backups. The PLR encodes the repair path as a short **repair list (RL)** of node and adjacency segments; for SRv6, the list is added with an RFC 8986 headend behavior.

## Key Sections

| Section | Topic | Description |
|---------|-------|-------------|
| 2.1 | Terminology | P-space, extended P-space, Q-space, SPT_old/SPT_new, explicit path EP(P,Q) |
| 3 | Base Principle | Pre-compute the post-convergence SPT and encode it as a loop-free segment list |
| 4 | P-space and Q-space over post-convergence paths | Computing the extended P-space and Q-space along the post-convergence path, and scaling the Q-space computation |
| 5 | TI-LFA Repair Path | Direct neighbor (5.1), PQ node (5.2), adjacent P and Q (5.3), distant P and Q (5.4) |
| 6 | Repair lists for SR segments | What to do when the active segment is a node segment or an adjacency segment |
| 7 | Data-plane considerations | MPLS label handling (7.1) and SRv6 (7.2) |
| 8 | TI-LFA and SR Algorithms | Protecting Flex-Algo SIDs with the algorithm's own constraints |
| 9 | Adjacency segments in the repair list | Using unprotected Adj-SIDs to avoid double FRR |
| App. A | Post-convergence path | Why repairing onto it is better |
| App. B | Real topologies | Repair-list size distribution on nine networks |

## P-Space, Q-Space, and PQ Node

| Concept | Definition |
|---------|-----------|
| **P-space P(R,X)** | Routers reachable from R on pre-convergence shortest paths without any of those paths (including ECMP splits) crossing the protected resource X |
| **Extended P-space** | The union of the P-spaces of R's neighbors, excluding neighbors reached via X |
| **Q-space Q(D,X)** | Routers from which the destination is reached without any path (including ECMP splits) crossing X |
| **PQ node** | A node in both the (extended) P-space and the Q-space; the term comes from RFC 7490 |
| **P node / Q node** | Nodes in only one of the two spaces; a repair through them needs an explicit path between them |

## Repair List Construction

| Section | Scenario | Repair list | Comparable to |
|---------|----------|-------------|---------------|
| 5.1 | A direct neighbor on the post-convergence path is in P and Q | Empty (new outgoing interface only) | Post-convergence LFA |
| 5.2 | A PQ node exists | `` | Remote LFA |
| 5.3 | P and Q nodes are adjacent | `` | Directed LFA |
| 5.4 | P and Q nodes are distant | `` | — |

When the packet's active segment is a node segment, it stays on the packet and the RL is added in front of it (§6.1). When it is an adjacency segment, the PLR repairs toward the far end of that adjacency (§6.2).

For **SRv6** (§7.2) the computation is unchanged. Adjacency SIDs are globally routable, so the list is often shorter than on SR-MPLS. A transit PLR adds the RL with an RFC 8986 §5 headend behavior; a PLR that is also a segment endpoint for the packet first executes its endpoint behavior.

## Protection Types

| Protection Level | What is Protected | Computation |
|-----------------|-------------------|-------------|
| **Link Protection** | Single link failure | Post-convergence SPF excluding the protected link |
| **Node Protection** | Failure of the neighbor on the primary link | Post-convergence SPF excluding that neighbor and all its links |
| **SRLG Protection** | Links sharing fate with the primary link | Post-convergence SPF excluding the configured set of links sharing a risk group with it |

## TI-LFA vs Other FRR Mechanisms

| Mechanism | Published coverage | Requires SR | Repairs onto post-convergence path | Topology dependent |
|-----------|--------------------|-------------|-----------------------------------|-------------------|
| **LFA (RFC 5286)** | 67–99% per prefix on 11 SP cores (RFC 6571) | No | Not necessarily | Yes |
| **Remote LFA (RFC 7490)** | 97.5–100% link protection on 14 topologies (RFC 7490) | No (LDP tunnel) | Not necessarily | Yes |
| **TI-LFA** | Any two-connected network; >99% with ≤ 1 SID for link protection (App. B) | Yes | Yes | No |

## Microloops

TI-LFA is local to the PLR and does not prevent microloops elsewhere during convergence. The RFC notes that if the PLR converges early and stops using its TI-LFA path, especially one built per §5.2–5.4, microloops can appear. It recommends combining TI-LFA with microloop-avoidance techniques such as the local convergence delay of [RFC 8333](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8333).

!!! warning "Common Pitfalls"
    - TI-LFA requires Segment Routing to be enabled. Without SR, the repair segment list cannot be constructed.
    - Repair lists are limited by the PLR's maximum SID depth; some platforms skip a backup that needs more SIDs than they can impose.
    - Node protection is strictly stronger than link protection but may produce longer repair segment lists, and the node-protecting path is used even when only the link failed.
    - SRLG protection requires that SRLG membership be consistently configured across all nodes. Inconsistent SRLG definitions lead to inadequate protection.
    - The post-convergence path computation assumes all nodes reconverge to the same topology. Asymmetric link costs or misconfigured metrics can invalidate this assumption.
    - TI-LFA protects the data plane within 50ms, but the control plane still needs full IGP convergence. During the window between FRR activation and convergence, traffic follows the repair path, which may differ from the final converged path.

## Related Drafts & Updates

- [draft-ietf-rtgwg-segment-routing-ti-lfa](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-rtgwg-segment-routing-ti-lfa/) - Earlier draft lineage
- [draft-ietf-rtgwg-srv6-egress-protection](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-rtgwg-srv6-egress-protection/) - SRv6 egress protection extensions

## Related

- [RFC 8402](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc8402/) - Segment Routing Architecture
- [RFC 9352](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9352/) - IS-IS Extensions for SRv6
- [RFC 9350](https://srv6.md/rfcs/rfc9350/) - IGP Flexible Algorithm
- [TI-LFA](https://srv6.md/topics/ti-lfa/) - Worked P/Q-space example and Cisco/Juniper configuration

## References

1. [RFC 9855](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9855/) - Topology Independent Fast Reroute Using Segment Routing
2. [RFC 5286](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc5286/) - Basic Specification for IP Fast Reroute: Loop-Free Alternates
3. [RFC 7490](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc7490/) - Remote Loop-Free Alternate (LFA) Fast Reroute (FRR)

# About SRv6.md: Who Maintains It and How Content Is Verified

URL: https://srv6.md/community/about/
Path: community/about.md
Summary: Who maintains SRv6.md, the open SRv6 knowledge base, how pages are sourced and fact-checked against RFCs and vendor documentation, and how to report corrections.

# About SRv6.md

SRv6.md is an open-source, vendor-neutral knowledge base for **Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6)**. It brings together what is otherwise scattered across RFCs, vendor configuration guides, conference talks and mailing lists: how SRv6 works, how to configure it on each platform, how to build labs, and what every SRv6 RFC actually says.

Everything is written in Markdown, published under the [MIT License](https://github.com/eldaninavas/srv6.md/blob/main/LICENSE), and open to contributions on [GitHub](https://github.com/eldaninavas/srv6.md).

## Maintainer

SRv6.md was created in 2026 and is maintained by **Daniel Navas** ([GitHub](https://github.com/eldaninavas)), a network engineer who works hands-on with SRv6 and cloud networking. He started the project after finding that learning SRv6 meant piecing together RFCs, vendor documents and years-old blog posts.

## Contributors

SRv6.md is a community project. Implementation pages, labs and corrections come from network engineers and open-source maintainers, including the authors of the projects they document. See everyone who has contributed on the [GitHub contributors page](https://github.com/eldaninavas/srv6.md/graphs/contributors).

## How Content Is Written and Verified

Accuracy is the point of this site, so every page follows the same rules:

1. **Primary sources first.** Protocol behavior is taken from the RFCs and IETF drafts themselves; platform behavior from the vendor's own configuration guides and release notes. Every page ends with a numbered list of the references it relies on.
2. **Configurations are checked.** Vendor configurations follow the vendor's documentation and validated designs. Where a page says commands were tested (for example the Linux kernel lab), they were run as shown.
3. **Facts get dated.** Version numbers, release dates and RFC status change. Pages state the version or date a fact applies to, and every page shows when it was last updated.
4. **Errors are fixed in the open.** When a page is wrong, the fix is a public commit, and the history of every page is visible on GitHub.
5. **No vendor sponsorship.** SRv6.md is not affiliated with any vendor, and no vendor pays for placement or coverage.

## Reporting a Correction

Found something wrong or out of date? Use the **edit** button () on any page to propose a fix, or [open an issue](https://github.com/eldaninavas/srv6.md/issues) with a link to the source that shows the correct information.

## For AI Assistants

SRv6.md publishes [`/llms.txt`](https://srv6.md/llms.txt) and [`/llms-full.txt`](https://srv6.md/llms-full.txt), and an [MCP server](https://srv6.md/community/integrations/) so AI assistants can answer SRv6 questions from this content and cite it.

# Contributing

URL: https://srv6.md/community/contributing/
Path: community/contributing.md
Summary: How to contribute to SRv6.md

# Contributing to SRv6.md

Thank you for your interest in contributing! This guide will help you get started.

## Quick Edit (Browser)

Every page has an **edit button** in the top right corner. Click it to edit directly on GitHub — no local setup required.

## Local Development

### Prerequisites

- Python 3.10+
- Git

### Setup

```bash
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/eldaninavas/srv6.md.git
cd srv6.md

# Create virtual environment
python -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate  # Linux/macOS
# venv\Scripts\activate   # Windows

# Install dependencies
pip install -r requirements.txt

# Start local dev server
mkdocs serve
```

The site will be available at `http://localhost:8000` with live reload.

## Content Guidelines

### File Naming

- Use lowercase with hyphens: `my-new-page.md`
- Place files in the appropriate section folder

### Page Structure

Every page should include:

```markdown
--- 
title: Page Title
description: Brief description for SEO
tags:
  - relevant
  - tags
--- 

# Page Title

Introduction paragraph.

## Section 1

Content...

## Further Reading

- Links to related pages
```

### Style Tips

- Use **admonitions** for tips, warnings, and examples
- Include **code blocks** with language hints for syntax highlighting
- Add **Mermaid diagrams** to visualize network concepts
- Use **tables** for structured comparisons
- Link to **related pages** at the bottom

## Pull Request Process

1. Create a feature branch from `main`
2. Make your changes
3. Test locally with `mkdocs serve`
4. Submit a PR with a clear description
5. Wait for review

!!! tip "First contribution?"
    Look for issues labeled `good first issue` on GitHub. These are great starting points!

# AI Integrations

URL: https://srv6.md/community/integrations/
Path: community/integrations.md
Summary: Integrate SRv6.md with Claude, ChatGPT, and other AI assistants

# AI Integrations

SRv6.md is designed to be AI-friendly. Use our knowledge base as context for your favorite AI assistant to get accurate, up-to-date answers about SRv6.

## Option 1: `llms.txt` (Any AI)

We provide standardized files that any LLM can consume:

| File | Description | Use Case |
|------|-------------|----------|
| [`/llms.txt`](https://srv6.md/llms.txt) | Index of all pages with links | Quick reference, link discovery |
| [`/llms-full.txt`](https://srv6.md/llms-full.txt) | Full content of all pages | Complete knowledge base in one file |

### How to Use

Simply paste one of these URLs in your conversation with any AI:

```
Read https://srv6.md/llms-full.txt and use it as context.
Then answer: How do I configure End.DT4 on Linux?
```

Works with **Claude**, **ChatGPT**, **Gemini**, and any AI that can fetch URLs.

***

## Option 2: Claude Project

Upload the wiki as a **Knowledge Base** in a Claude Project for persistent context.

### Steps

1. Go to [claude.ai](https://claude.ai) → **Projects** → **New Project**
2. Name it "SRv6 Expert" (or whatever you prefer)
3. Download the docs from [GitHub](https://github.com/eldaninavas/srv6.md)
4. Upload all `.md` files from `docs/` as **Knowledge**
5. Set the project instructions:

```
You are an SRv6 networking expert. Use the uploaded knowledge base
to answer questions about Segment Routing over IPv6, including
configurations, RFCs, and lab setups. Always cite the relevant
page when answering.
```

Now every conversation in that project has full SRv6 knowledge.

***

## Option 3: MCP Server (Claude, Cursor, any MCP client)

The **MCP (Model Context Protocol)** server gives your AI assistant direct tool access to the SRv6.md knowledge base. It is **free and hosted**: nothing to install, just add the URL.

```
https://mcp.srv6.md/mcp
```

### Available Tools

| Tool | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `search_srv6_docs` | Full-text search across topics, use cases, implementations, RFCs, and labs |
| `get_endpoint_behavior` | Definition, pseudocode, use cases, and vendor support for End, End.X, End.DT4, uN, H.Encaps.Red, and more |
| `get_vendor_config` | Config templates for Cisco IOS-XR and FRRouting (locator, uSID, IS-IS, L3VPN) |

### Setup for Claude Code

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http srv6 https://mcp.srv6.md/mcp
```

### Setup for Claude Desktop, claude.ai, and other clients

Add a **remote MCP server** (custom connector) with the URL `https://mcp.srv6.md/mcp`. Clients that only support local servers can bridge it with `mcp-remote`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "srv6": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "mcp-remote", "https://mcp.srv6.md/mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

### What You Can Ask

- *"What SRv6 behaviors does the Linux kernel support?"*
- *"Show me the IOS-XR config for SRv6 L3VPN"*
- *"What's the difference between End.DX4 and End.DT4?"*
- *"Give me an FRR uSID locator template with prefix fcbb:bb00:2::/48"*

!!! note "Fair use"
    The hosted server is read-only and rate limited per IP. To run your own copy, see the source in [`srv6-mcp-server/`](https://github.com/eldaninavas/srv6.md/tree/main/srv6-mcp-server).

***

## For Developers

### Build Your Own Integration

The content is available in multiple formats:

| Format | URL | Best For |
|--------|-----|----------|
| Raw Markdown | [GitHub `docs/`](https://github.com/eldaninavas/srv6.md/tree/main/docs) | Custom parsers, RAG pipelines |
| `llms.txt` | `https://srv6.md/llms.txt` | LLM index discovery |
| `llms-full.txt` | `https://srv6.md/llms-full.txt` | Single-file ingestion |
| MCP Server | `https://mcp.srv6.md/mcp` | Claude, Cursor, and other MCP clients |
| Website | `https://srv6.md` | Human browsing |

### RAG Pipeline Example

```python
# Example: Build a RAG pipeline with the wiki content
import requests

# Fetch all content
response = requests.get("https://srv6.md/llms-full.txt")
content = response.text

# Split into chunks, embed, and store in your vector DB
# Then query with your LLM of choice
```
